Foreword A troubling paradox is taking shape across the global financing landscape. Access to international finance has improved, but the price of that finance has not. Low- and middle-income countries are borrowing more, paying more, and, in many cases, leaving less for long-term development.

The numbers are striking. In 2025, external debt across low- and middle-income countries surged 5.5 percent to a record $9.4 trillion, the largest annual increase in four years. Private lenders returned, bond markets reopened, and governments found new paths to financing that had been closed off during the preceding years of rate tightening and risk aversion. On the surface, this looks like a recovery. Beneath the headline numbers, however, a more complicated picture emerges. The return to international capital markets has been highly uneven. The poorest and most vulnerable countries face borrowing costs not seen since the late 1980s. Low- and middle-income countries’ total debt service burden rose for a fifth consecutive year in 2025, which means that more public resources are being absorbed by servicing debt at a time when countries need to invest more in infrastructure, jobs, education, health, and the foundations of long-term growth. Continued borrowing through international bond markets in 2026, despite elevated yields, raises important questions about whether the terms are sustainable and whether the capital raised is reaching the people and places that need it most.

This question has become more urgent in a global economy increasingly prone to shocks. Over the past decade, countries have confronted a pandemic, disruption to trade and supply chains, a sharp increase in food and energy prices, geopolitical fragmentation, and repeated episodes of financial market volatility. Such shocks are difficult for any economy to absorb. It is harder still when governments already face substantial financing needs and limited room to respond. The consequences extend beyond government balance sheets, as debt vulnerabilities are not simply a financial concern. When debt service constrains productive and social spending, the consequences can ultimately reach households through weaker investment, fewer opportunities, and greater vulnerability to shocks. For example, the report finds that, during periods of external shocks, xi

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 countries with heavier debt burdens tend to experience larger adverse changes in the share of people unable to afford a healthy diet. Against this backdrop, knowing how much countries owe, to whom, and on what terms has never been more important.

For more than five decades, the World Bank Group has worked with borrowing countries to build the most comprehensive source of comparable external debt data for developing economies. But transparency cannot rest on debtor reporting alone. A major advance in recent years has been the systematic reconciliation of loan-by-loan information reported by borrowers through the World Bank Group’s Debtor Reporting System with corresponding records provided by bilateral creditors. The results show what cooperation between borrowers and creditors can achieve. Since the creditor data-sharing exercise began in 2022, successive rounds have helped reconcile loan-level records, identify discrepancies, validate information, and close critical data gaps, strengthening the quality and consistency of external debt statistics. This is debt transparency in practice. It is not simply about publishing more data. It is about comparing borrowers’ and creditors’ records, identifying inconsistencies, resolving differences, and progressively improving the common information base on which debt decisions are made.

That work becomes even more important as sovereign financing grows more complex. New creditors, instruments, guarantees, restructurings, and financing arrangements can make it harder to establish a complete picture of a country’s obligations. Without reliable and reconciled information, governments cannot manage debt effectively, creditors cannot assess risks accurately, and debt restructurings can become more difficult. Transparency is a shared responsibility. Borrowers must maintain comprehensive and timely debt records; creditors, official and private, should disclose the information needed to understand those obligations; and international institutions must strengthen standards, close data gaps, and support stronger debt management systems.

Better information must ultimately lead to better financing. Countries bearing some of the greatest development burdens continue to face some of the steepest borrowing costs, a paradox that compounds their disadvantages at every turn. Financing that merely enables countries to roll over costly debt cannot substitute for financing that expands productive capacity and raises future incomes. The objective should, therefore, not be more debt. It should be better financing that is affordable, transparent, sustainable, and capable of supporting investment and growth. xii

Foreword The message of this year’s report is clear: access to finance is not enough. We must know the debt, understand its terms, and ensure that the financing developing economies receive strengthens rather than constrains their ability to grow, withstand shocks, and improve the lives of their people. Key Takeaways Borrowing by low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) surged in 2025, marking the sharpest increase in external debt in four years and a forceful return of private creditors to developing country markets. External debt climbed to a record $9.4 trillion as bond issues rebounded, the US dollar weakened, and investors again showed greater willingness to lend. But the reopening of capital markets came at a steep price, especially for the poorest countries, which faced some of their highest borrowing costs in decades. Debt service payments also rose for a fifth consecutive year. Even so, stronger economic growth helped stabilize some debt ratios, and net long-term debt transfers turned positive after years of outflows.

• Debt accumulation accelerated sharply in 2025. The external debt of LMICs jumped 5.5 percent to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, the fastest increase since 2021 and more than four times the average annual growth recorded from 2022 to 2024. The increase in external debt was even faster for countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) financing, rising 8.1 percent to $1.3 trillion, and for low-income countries, climbing 8.9 percent to $262.4 billion, the biggest increase since 2020.

• A weakening dollar amplified the rise in debt. The dramatic depreciation of the US dollar during the year accounted for 28.2 percent of the increase in LMICs’ external public and publicly guaranteed debt. This outcome reflects an important valuation effect: International Debt Statistics are expressed in US dollars for comparability, including liabilities denominated in other currencies. For several of the largest borrowers from concessional windows, currency valuation gains in 2025 not only offset principal payments made during the year but also, in some cases, partially reversed the stock reductions achieved through repayments in 2024, leaving reported balances higher at end-2025 despite continued debt servicing.

• Private creditors returned to LMICs. Private lending, which is more susceptible to fluctuations in financial market conditions, pricing conditions, and perceived creditworthiness of borrowers, saw a strong rebound in 2025. LMIC debt stock owed to private creditors increased 5.2 percent in 2025 to $5.0 trillion, a significant acceleration from the 0.6 percent increase recorded in 2024. This increase was due to a combined increase in debt owed to bondholders and debt owed to commercial banks and other private xvii

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 creditors, which increased by 5.7 percent (to $2.4 trillion) and 4.7 percent (to $2.7 trillion), respectively. LMIC economies, measured by gross national income, grew by 5.1 percent in 2025. This strong economic growth encouraged lenders to return to these countries, and many LMIC governments were willing to borrow despite relatively high interest rates. • The countries that can least afford it are paying the most to borrow. Increased borrowing from private creditors hardened lending terms disproportionately for IDA-eligible countries, which faced an average interest rate of 8.2 percent on new commitments during the year, the highest since the late 1980s. The difference in interest rates that this group of borrowers pays when borrowing from official creditors and rates on debt from private creditors widened significantly over the past decade, from 3.4 percentage points in 2016 to 5.5 percentage points in 2025. International Bank for Reconstruction and Development borrowers, by contrast, saw improvements in the terms on new commitments, with an improved 5.5 percent average interest rate, down from 5.8 percent the previous year.

• The bond market reopened for LMICs. After being essentially shut out of international bond markets for several years, LMICs returned to bond markets in force in 2025. LMICs’ public sector bond issuances accounted for 68.1 percent of new disbursements in 2025, increasing 34.6 percent to $250.6 billion, the largest volume since 2021, and reflective of a robust return of investor confidence. • LMICs maintained market access in 2026, but at higher costs. Preliminary data for January through August of 2026 show no signs of a slowdown in LMICs’ bond market activity, with many countries already exceeding their full-year 2025 issuance volumes. This continued activity comes amid a backdrop of elevated global borrowing costs and tightened financial conditions in 2026. Borrowing costs for the most vulnerable countries remained elevated and even rose in some cases.

• Debt service burdens remain a pressure point for LMICs. Total debt service payments (interest plus principal) rose for the fifth year in a row, increasing 1.9 percent to $1.4 trillion in 2025. Payments to private creditors drove the increase, with payments to bondholders rising 13.7 percent to $363.1 billion. Between 2022 and 2025, LMICs paid about $436.1 billion more in debt service than they received in new financing. However, the trend reversed in 2025: long-term debt flows shifted from a net outflow of $118.4 billion in 2024 to a net inflow of $45.4 billion. xviii

KEy TAKEAwAyS • Debt burdens eased in IDA-eligible countries but rose elsewhere. Despite a sharp increase in borrowing, IDA-eligible countries saw their external debt burdens decline slightly in 2025. Their debt-to-income ratio fell from 42.1 percent to 41.2 percent, as economic growth outpaced debt accumulation, and some countries benefited from debt restructuring. The picture was different for other developing economies. Excluding China, LMICs saw their debt-to-income ratio rise to 34.5 percent, as debt grew faster than national income. • Other financial flows to LMICs continue to diverge, with negative consequences. Foreign direct investment (FDI) and personal remittances to LMICs continued to diverge in 2025, a trend that has been accelerating over two decades. LMICs saw their FDI contract by 25.5 percent from 2011 to 2025, whereas remittances more than doubled over the period. In 2025, remittances were about $294.5 billion more than FDI. This growing divide carries long-term implications for growth, because FDI builds productive capacity whereas remittances primarily support households and remain less connected to productive investment.

In addition to the release of the 2025 external debt data from the International Debt Statistics database, this edition of the International Debt Report provides • An analysis of macroeconomic conditions and risks LMICs face amid changing global financial and trade conditions and what these shifts imply for these countries’ debt burdens and vulnerabilities; • A discussion of how rising debt service burdens, elevated financing needs, and changing financing patterns are constraining fiscal space and intensifying debt and rollover risks, as well as the policy priorities for strengthening resilience; • An analysis of how elevated debt burdens appear to be associated with adverse changes in healthy diet unaffordability in LMICs during periods of global stress and of potential underlying mechanisms, including food import reliance and diversification; and • An update on progress of the debt transparency agenda and the role of the World Bank Group in advancing sound debt management and policy frameworks, enhancing the accuracy and coverage of debt data, and promoting the reconciliation of borrower and creditor accounts. xix

1. Analysis of External Debt Stocks and Debt Flows as of End-2025 Trends in External Debt, 2015–25 Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a rebound in lending from private creditors.

That rebound, driven by both new borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten. (Refer to box 1.1 for definitions of debt terms used in this report.) 3

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Box 1.1 External Debt Data: Concepts, Sources, and Coverage This report presents data and analysis on external debt for 119 low- and middle-income countries and Guyana. The primary source for these data is reports to the World Bank Group’s Debtor Reporting System (DRS) from member countries that have received either International Bank for Reconstruction and Development loans or International Development Association credits, and that have outstanding obligations to the World Bank Group. The DRS, instituted in 1951, has its origins in the World Bank Group’s need to monitor and assess the financial position of its borrowers. Comprehensive information on data sources and the methodology used to compile the statistics presented in this report can be found in the appendix under “Data Sources.” The following describes the key concepts and data sources. • The DRS follows international standards and defines external debt as the outstanding amount of actual current liabilities in both domestic and foreign currency that require payment(s) of principal and/or interest by the debtor at (Box continues on next page) 4

The sum of principal and interest payments is defined as debt service. • The total external debt of a country is the sum of public and publicly guaranteed debt, private nonguaranteed debt, and short-term debt. • Public and publicly guaranteed external debt comprises long-term external obligations (maturities of over one year) of all public debtors, including debt held by the central government and by state-owned enterprises. Data are collected on a loan-by-loan basis through the DRS. Reporting countries submit quarterly reports on new loan commitments and annual reports on loan status and transactions (new commitments, gross disbursements, principal, and interest payments).

• Private nonguaranteed debt comprises long-term external obligations of private debtors that are not guaranteed by a public entity. The DRS has covered private nonguaranteed debt since 1973; however, for this category of debt data, the annual status and transactions (gross disbursements, principal, and interest payments) are reported in aggregate. • Short-term debt is defined as debt with an original maturity of one year or less and is not covered under DRS reporting requirements. However, most DRS reporters provide an annual report on outstanding short-term debt stocks on a voluntary basis. For countries that do not provide these data, information on their short-term debt is drawn from the Quarterly External Debt Statistics database, a joint World Bank Group–International Monetary Fund initiative, wherein data are compiled and reported by countries’ central banks, along with data compiled by the Bank for International Settlements.

All debt data reported to the DRS are validated against—and, when appropriate, supplemented by—data from other sources. These additional data include the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position statistics, Quarterly External Debt Statistics, information published on official government websites, reports from the International Monetary Fund, regional development banks, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the Bank for International Settlements, and websites and annual publications of lending agencies. The rate of LMIC external debt accumulation in 2025 was comparable to the years 2019 and 2020, but it is above the more recent annual average increase of 0.5 percent during the 2022–24 period. Long-term external debt stock rose 6.1 percent to $7.0 trillion, equivalent to 74.3 percent of the total external debt stock, driven by a 7.6 percent rise in long-term external public and publicly 5

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 guaranteed (PPG) debt, including obligations to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and a much smaller 3.8 percent increase in private nonguaranteed (PNG) external debt (debt obligations of private borrowers that are not backed by a government or public sector guarantee). The return of debt accumulation to 2019–20 levels indicates both continued support from multilateral creditors and a significant rebound of private investor confidence and lending, as well as LMICs’ eagerness to take advantage of times when international investors are willing to lend. In addition, the short-term debt stock of LMICs increased 4.0 percent to $2.4 trillion at end-2025. These obligations, which are composed of liabilities with a maturity of one year or less and interest arrears on long term debt, stood for 25.7 percent of total external debt, a share that has remained stable over the past decade for LMICs.

Debt increased across both low- and middle-income countries. In low-income countries (LICs), it rose 8.9 percent to $262.4 billion. In MICs, debt rose 5.4 percent to a record $9.2 trillion in 2025, the fastest increase since 2021. The rise was striking because China, which accounts for nearly one-quarter of LMIC debt, continued to reduce its borrowing. China’s external debt fell by 4.3 percent to $2.3 trillion (figure 1.1), which means that debt accumulated substantially faster across other MICs than the overall MIC figure suggests. 6

text: 1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 When China is excluded, the cumulative external debt stock of MICs increased at a much faster pace—by 9.1 percent in 2025, to $6.9 trillion in 2025. An increase of that magnitude has not been seen since 2017 and was concentrated among the 10 largest LMIC borrowers other than China.1 These borrowers account for 59.5 percent of all LMIC external debt. Half of them recorded double-digit increases in their borrowing levels in 2025, led by a 29.2 percent increase in Ukraine’s debt stock, to $250.3 billion, following continued and unprecedented support from the Group of Seven countries and multilateral creditors. Argentina, Colombia, South Africa, and Türkiye also experienced double-digit increases in their external debt positions. External debt stock of the other five MICs among the top 10 borrowers (again, excluding China) also rose, increasing by 7.0 percent to $2.7 trillion in 2025, with short-term debt stock rising at a rate of 8.8 percent, and long-term debt at a rate of 6.7 percent. These five countries accounted for 29.6 percent of MIC total debt stock.

Some of these countries also turned to complex liability management operations to transform the profile of their debt portfolios, as well as total return swap operations, which have gained prominence for LMICs (refer to box 1.2 for definitions and country-specific use of total return swaps). Box 1.2 Total Return Swaps: An Emerging Form of Sovereign Financing Total return swaps (TRSs) have traditionally been used in financial markets to transfer the economic risks and returns of an underlying asset without transferring its legal ownership. More recently, TRS structures have gained prominence as a form of sovereign financing, often involving up-front funding and the pledging of government securities or other assets as collateral.

How a TRS Works A TRS is a financial derivative contract in which one party transfers the total economic return of a reference asset, including income and changes in market value, to another party in exchange for a predetermined stream of payments, typically linked to a benchmark interest rate plus a spread. In sovereign transactions, TRS structures can combine derivative features with financing. This combination can blur the distinction between a financial derivative and conventional borrowing, and makes it important to assess the economic substance of the transaction. Sovereign borrowers may turn to TRS arrangements when conventional market financing is unavailable, slow, or prohibitively expensive. By using government (Box continues on next page) 7

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Box 1.2 Total Return Swaps: An Emerging Form of Sovereign Financing (continued) securities as collateral, borrowers can obtain foreign currency liquidity quickly and potentially at a lower short-term financing rate. These benefits, however, come with substantial collateral requirements, margin-call, refinancing, and transparency risks.

The Growing Use of TRSs in Sovereign Financing Since 2024, TRS arrangements have been identified in Angola, Argentina, Colombia, Nigeria, and Senegal, with financing amounts ranging from about $1.0 billion to $9.3 billion. Maturities have generally ranged from one to three years, and disclosed collateralization ratios have typically been between 133 and 198 percent. Collateral has included domestic government securities, external sovereign bonds, US Treasury securities, or combinations of these instruments. The transactions vary considerably in scale and collateral structure. In Argentina, the central bank entered a $3 billion, three-year TRS in 2025 backed by domestic government securities, although the collateralization ratio has not been publicly disclosed. Angola entered a $1.2 billion, one-year transaction in 2024 collateralized at 198 percent, equivalent to about $2.4 billion in collateral, primarily external sovereign bonds. In 2025, this financing was extended and increased to $1.5 billion for three years, with collateralization reduced to 148 percent, or approximately $2.2 billion.

Angola also entered a separate $1 billion, three-year transaction in 2025 collateralized at 140 percent, using a combination of US Treasuries and domestic government securities. Larger transactions demonstrate the potential scale of this financing. In Colombia, TRS transactions totaling approximately $9.3 billion in 2025 had a one-year maturity and collateralization of about 160 percent, implying approximately $15.1 billion in pledged external and domestic government securities. Nigeria’s $5 billion transaction in 2026 has a three-year maturity and collateralization of approximately 133 percent, corresponding to about $6.7 billion in domestic securities. In Senegal, seven TRS transactions contracted in 2025 provided approximately $1.1 billion in financing with three-year maturities and average collateralization of about 135 percent, corresponding to approximately $1.5 billion in pledged domestic government securities. Common Features of Sovereign TRS Financing The recent transactions point to three common features: • Large financing amounts: Transactions range from about $1.0 billion to $9.3 billion. (Box continues on next page) 8

1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 Box 1.2 Total Return Swaps: An Emerging Form of Sovereign Financing (continued) • Significant overcollateralization: For every $1.00 of financing received, disclosed arrangements have involved securities worth approximately $1.33 to $1.98. • Relatively short maturities: Maturities of one to three years can create significant refinancing needs when transactions come due.

Implications for Debt Statistics and Transparency A TRS is normally a financial derivative, but some structures can also create debt. If the sovereign receives cash up front and is required to repay it regardless of the performance of the underlying assets, the financing creates an unconditional repayment obligation and is therefore recorded as debt. The derivative component is recorded separately. Securities pledged as collateral generally remain on the sovereign’s balance sheet and do not create additional debt simply because they are pledged. The growing use of TRS financing also raises broader transparency and risk-management issues. Headline debt statistics may not fully reveal the amount of collateral pledged, exposure to margin calls, or refinancing and liquidity risks. Transparent reporting should therefore provide information on the amount financed, maturity, collateralization ratio and type of collateral, margin requirements, repayment obligations, and rollover or early termination provisions, while separately identifying the financing and derivative components.

External debt, which is usually contracted and denominated in foreign currency, is exposed to year-on-year and intrayear exchange rate fluctuations that affect its rate of accumulation and its debt service payments. Movements in the value of the US dollar against other global currencies affect the value of LMICs’ debt, and the size of these fluctuations in 2025 had important implications for LMICs, particularly those with large dollar-denominated external debt portfolios. For this subset of countries following a flexible exchange rate regime, dollar-denominated debt became cheaper to service.

Additionally, in this publication, the US dollar is used as the common currency by convention to measure all external borrowing of LMICs, which has implications over time. As the US dollar depreciated in 2025 against the euro, the British pound, the Chinese yuan, and many other currencies, the debt stock denominated in those currencies increased when converted to US dollars. The euro, IMF special drawing rights (SDR),2 the Chinese yuan, and the Japanese yen are the four currencies that make up the largest portion of LMICs’ non-dollar-denominated debt. In 2025 the dollar depreciated 13.1 percent against the euro, 5.0 percent against SDR, and 4.4 percent against the yuan, and remained essentially stable against the weakened 9

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Japanese yen. The dollar’s dramatic 2025 depreciation inflates the size of external debt denominated in these currencies; that debt would appear to be more moderate if, for example, it was recorded in euros or other hard currencies. The effect is particularly pronounced among the concessional arm of all multilateral creditors. SDR-denominated loans represent a significant share of outstanding concessional debt across multilateral institutions, and the dollar’s 5.0 percent depreciation against the SDR in 2025 increased these loans’ dollar-equivalent values correspondingly. Concessional repayment schedules further amplify the impact: because annual principal payments are small relative to outstanding balances, the dollar-equivalent currency revaluation of the debt stock tends to outweigh the modest stock reductions from debt servicing.

For several of the largest borrowers from concessional windows, currency valuation gains in 2025 not only offset principal payments made during the year but also, in some cases, partially reversed the stock reductions achieved through repayments in 2024, leaving reported balances higher at end-2025 despite continued debt servicing. Of the $301.8 billion increase in LMICs’ PPG debt stock (external debt obligations of a country’s government and any private sector debts backed by a public sector guarantee) recorded in 2025, at least 28.2 percent can be attributed to the depreciation of the US dollar. Borrowing by the PPG sector of the economy gets reported at the instrument level and in the currency in which the liabilities are denominated or repaid. Accordingly, this level of detailed reporting makes possible the computation of the effect of the cross-currency valuation. Viewed from a lending category perspective, the external debt stock of countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) financing increased 8.1 percent in 2025, to $1.3 trillion.

Of this group, LICs’ debt increased at an even faster pace of 8.9 percent in 2025, to $262.4 billion, a marked increase not seen since 2020. Although LICs account for only a 2.8 percent share of total LMIC debt stock, over 60 percent of these countries are at high risk of debt distress or already in debt distress. An increase of such magnitude for this most vulnerable group of countries exacerbates their susceptibility to financial market volatility and stresses their already limited fiscal space. (Refer to box 1.3 for income and lending classifications.) Private lending, which is more susceptible to fluctuations in financial market conditions, pricing conditions, and perceived creditworthiness of the borrower, saw a strong rebound in 2025. LMIC debt stock owed to private creditors increased 5.2 percent in 2025 to $5.0 trillion, compared to the 0.6 percent increase recorded in 2024. The increase in debt stock owed to private creditors was due to a combined increase in debt owed to bondholders and to commercial banks and other private creditors, which increased by 5.7 percent (to $2.4 trillion) and 4.7 percent (to $2.7 trillion), respectively (figure 1.2). 10

1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 Almost three-fourths of total LMIC debt stock owed to bondholders was issued by public sector entities; that share increased 6.2 percent in 2025, to $1.8 trillion. The increase is even more pronounced when China is excluded: debt stock owed to bondholders increased 11.1 percent, to $1.8 trillion, and debt stock owed to commercial banks and other private creditors rose 8.3 percent, to $2.3 trillion (figure 1.3). The increase in private lending, which is highly procyclical, was correlated with this group of countries’ robust economic growth, as measured by their gross national income (GNI), which grew 6.0 percent in 2025. Through the most recent crises, decreases in debt stock from this creditor base have been associated with the 2008 financial crisis, the 2015 turbulence, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The robust 2025 economic growth of LMICs (excluding China) attracted lenders back to these economies, and many LMIC governments proved eager to borrow when international investors are willing to lend, even at elevated borrowing rates.

For this group of countries, the share of debt stock owed to bondholders by public sector entities stands at 82 percent, a much higher share than the PNG sector counterpart, and increased by 10.4 percent to $1.5 trillion in 2025. The opposite is true for debt stock owed to commercial banks and other private creditors, where an 83 percent share of the obligations is held by the PNG sector of the economy. This type of debt increased 7.0 percent to $1.9 trillion in 2025, and the debt stock of public sector entities owed to commercial banks and other private creditors saw a much larger increase of 15.1 percent, to $385.7 billion in 2025. 11

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 LMICs’ debt stock owed to all other creditor groups also increased in 2025. Debt stock owed to official creditors (public institutions such as national governments and international organizations) increased 8.4 percent in 2025, to $2.0 trillion. Lending by official bilateral creditors (national governments and their agencies) also showed a comeback, increasing 4.7 percent in 2025 after a 3.4 percent retrenchment in 2024. Support from multilateral institutions such as the World Bank Group and the IMF continued to be positive in 2025, but at a decreasing pace when compared to the COVID-19 pandemic era. Except for the multilateral support to Ukraine provided under the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration Loans for Ukraine initiative, the cumulative countercyclical lending by these institutions decelerated in 2025. (Box 1.4 describes the international support for Ukraine through this initiative.) LMICs’ debt stock owed to multilateral creditors increased 9.6 percent to $1.5 trillion in 2025. However, when the European Union’s support to Ukraine is excluded, debt stock owed to multilateral creditors increased 7.0 percent to $1.4 trillion in 2026.

Box 1.4 International Support for Ukraine: The G-7 Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration A Surge in Lending, Concentrated Among Official Creditors Financial support for Ukraine from bilateral and multilateral creditors has reached unprecedented levels since the start of the Ukraine War in February 2022. Official creditors, including the Group of Seven (G-7) bilateral creditors and multilaterals like the European Union and the World Bank Group, provided $122.2 billion in disbursements during the 2022–25 period. This support reshaped the composition of Ukraine’s external debt (figure B1.4.1). Long-term external debt stock rose from $99 billion in 2015 to $227 billion in 2025, but little of that increase was driven by private creditors, whose claims remained broadly flat over the past decade, rising slightly from $72 billion to $82 billion. Debt owed to multilateral creditors accounts for most of the increase. Bilateral claims increased sixfold over the past decade but grew from a much smaller base and remained a modest share of the total.

These official creditors delivered support to Ukraine not only through direct lending but also through grants, trust funds, guarantees, and co- and parallel financing, among other financial instruments. The ERA and the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism One such distinct lending mechanism is the G-7 Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) Loans to Ukraine initiative, agreed in October 2024. Under the ERA, G-7 members committed approximately $50 billion in support to Ukraine. (Box continues on next page) 14
1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025

Box 1.4 International Support for Ukraine: The G-7 Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (continued) Figure B1.4.1 Ukraine’s Long-Term External Debt Stock, by Creditor Type, 2015–25 US$ (billion) 250 200 150 100 50 0 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025 Private creditors Multilateral creditors Bilateral creditors Source: World Bank Group International Debt Statistics database. What is unique about this mechanism, compared to direct lending, is that the principal and interest are serviced from future revenues generated by immobilized Russian sovereign assets rather than from Ukraine’s own budget. Those revenues are channeled through the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism, administered by the European Commission. ERA support extended as loans creates a repayment obligation for the government of Ukraine and is therefore recorded as an external debt liability, whereas the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism represents a financial asset of Ukraine available to service the loan.

Under the Debtor Reporting System and international statistical standards—the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, sixth and seventh editions (IMF 2009, 2025) and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014)— this loan is classified as a debt instrument based on the existence of a contractual obligation to repay principal and/or interest, rather than on the expected source of repayment. Accordingly, borrowing remains a debt liability even when debt service is expected to be financed from proceeds of immobilized or seized assets. Those proceeds provide the mechanism for repayment but do not change the nature of the liability. Only where repayment is legally limited to those proceeds and the borrower has no obligation to cover any shortfall would the arrangement require different statistical treatment. This single initiative therefore appears in the Debtor Reporting System through several different channels. The European Union’s Macro Financial Assistance loan (Box continues on next page) 15

Canada’s contribution (Can$5 billion) is recorded as bilateral debt. The United Kingdom’s contribution (£1.7 billion) is recorded as a commercial loan backed by UK Export Finance. The contributions of Japan and the United States were transferred to the World Bank Group–hosted Facilitation of Resources to Invest in Strengthening (F.O.R.T.I.S.) Ukraine Financial Intermediary Fund. This fund will provide grants to finance nonmilitary projects, programs, and activities supporting Ukraine’s macroeconomic stability, promoting the country’s reform agenda, and restoring debt sustainability, while remaining consistent with the International Monetary Fund’s supported programs. Because the financing is provided in the form of a grant, it does not create a repayment obligation and therefore does not give rise to an external debt liability.

Trends in External Debt Flows, 2015–25 Net debt inflows (disbursements minus principal repayments) to LMICs grew for a third consecutive year, more than doubling in 2025 to $423.5 billion. From a maturity standpoint, short-term net debt inflows recorded a more than fivefold increase in 2025, to $89.4 billion, and long-term net debt inflows doubled, to $334.1 billion, approximately 78.9 percent of the total volume of net inflows. This increase in long-term net debt inflows was due to the return to lending to LMICs by private creditors in 2025; these creditors accounted for 75.2 percent of the total long-term component and increased their lending volume by 180.5 percent to $251.1 billion. Private net debt flows are highly procyclical in nature, and the return of private investors has been highly correlated with LMICs’ ongoing economic growth since the COVID-19 downturn in 2020. In 2025, LMIC economies, as measured by their GNI, grew 5.1 percent, to a cumulative $40.2 trillion.

In 2025, net debt inflows from private creditors were nearly evenly divided between bond issuance and lending by commercial banks, at $130.4 billion and $120.7 billion, respectively. Net debt inflows from banks and other private creditors, which had retrenched 71.3 percent to $17.6 billion in 2024, saw the biggest increase, reaching volumes not seen since 2018. Although public sector borrowing from these creditors recorded a 19.4 percent decrease to $34.2 billion in 2025, the return was mostly attributed to the PNG sector of the economy, which recorded an inflow of $86.5 billion in 2025, a stark contrast from the outflow of $24.9 billion recorded in 2024. 16

1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 When China, which has recorded four consecutive years of net debt outflows, is excluded, LMICs’ net debt inflows increased to a record $527.6 billion in 2025 (figure 1.4). The yearly increase is more than twice the 2024 total volume and is due to record-high net debt inflows from private creditors, which accounted for 80.8 percent of long-term inflows. This group of countries’ net debt inflows from private creditors more than tripled in 2025, to $358.3 billion, with lending from both bondholders and commercial banks recording nearly threefold increases of $177.0 billion and $181.4 billion, respectively. PNG and PPG sector borrowers held an equal share of the volume of these inflows, but obligations to bondholders and commercial banks differed. Net debt inflows to public sector entities from bondholders accounted for 76.6 percent of inflows received from private creditors, at $137.7 billion in 2025, more than twice the volume recorded in the prior year.

Although holding a much smaller share, inflows from commercial banks and other private creditors to public sector entities increased at the same rate as bondholders, reaching $42.1 billion in 2025. The opposite is recorded for PNG net debt inflows, where inflows from bondholders stood for a 22.0 percent share (at $39.2 billion) of the total, and banks and other private creditors accounted for a 78.0 percent share (at $139.3 billion). In volume terms, these highs have not been seen since 2013. Essentially, public sector entities borrowed via bond markets whereas private sector borrowers used loans from banks and other private sector entities. 17

text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 The increase in private creditors’ net debt flows was driven by an increase in new disbursements accompanied by a slowdown in principal repayments over the same period. New disbursements from private creditors lending to the public sector increased 12.1 percent to $367.8 billion, whereas principal repayments decreased by 3.3 percent to $227.3 billion in 2025. Bond issuances accounted for 68.1 percent of these new disbursements, increasing 34.6 percent to $250.6 billion, to volumes not seen since 2021. Notably, when China is excluded, the $238.9 billion issuance is a record for LMICs, reflecting a robust return of investor confidence. The monetary tightening in advanced economies disproportionately affected the riskiest borrowers, and subsequent monetary easing helped improve market conditions and lower borrowing costs from their 2023 peaks. The rebound was substantial both in pace and scale. The increase in new public sector disbursements was driven by Mexico, which accounted for a 16.7 percent share of new LMIC issues, at $42.0 billion in 2025.
Türkiye and Colombia were the next largest LMIC public sector issuers, at $27.7 billion and $27.5 billion respectively, which reflects strong international investor demand in 2025.

The headline issuance figure masks a divergence of the use of the proceeds from these international bond sales, however. Some of the proceeds from new debt issuances in 2025 were strategically used to fund LMICs’ ongoing and proactive liability management strategies and operations, particularly debt buyback operations. Fourteen countries carried out such operations to prepay and mature $34.5 billion of their outstanding external debt obligations. The debt management strategies included the use of proceeds from the issuance of new bonds to mature existing liabilities and were part of larger operations, in efforts to alter the maturity structure of these countries’ debt portfolios, to change the currency in which the debt is denominated in order to reduce exchange rate exposure, or to lower the interest rates being charged. Bullet payments of bond obligations coming due over the 2024–26 redemption wall were pushed further into the future through these operations, easing rollover risk pressures.

In June and September of 2025, Mexico’s public sector executed several debt management operations, including issuing new international bonds to retire existing sovereign and state-owned enterprises’ liabilities for an equal or lesser nominal value. These buyback operations totaled $17.6 billion and aimed to extend the maturity profiles of existing liabilities and to lower borrowing costs by capturing lower interest rates. Other markets also recorded major buyback operations, with Colombia at $6.6 billion and Argentina at $2.8 billion, recording the second- and third-largest LMIC operations. Both countries used debt buyback operations in 2025 to retire existing bonds before maturity, with 18

1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 the goal of lengthening the maturity profiles of their portfolios and reducing the cost of servicing these obligations. In 2025, Kenya issued new bonds of $3.5 billion that were used to execute two debt buyback operations, the largest from an IDA-eligible country, at $1.2 billion. The proceeds were used to smooth the maturity profile of existing liabilities by refinancing near-term liabilities with longer-dated debt, including the $900 million Eurobond maturing in 2027 and the $1 billion Eurobond maturing in 2028. (Refer to the “Debt Reorganization, 2025” section for a more detailed discussion on the liability management operations implemented in 2025.) New bond issuance from the PNG sector of LMICs also increased in 2025, albeit at a slower pace of 18.7 percent and about half the volume of the PPG sector, at $132.3 billion (figure 1.5). These new issuances were concentrated among the top 10 LMIC borrowers, many of which are in Latin America and the Caribbean. Although lower than in 2024, new bond issuance from China’s PNG sector was the largest among LMICs in 2025, at $36.9 billion.

Türkiye and Brazil were the second- and third-largest issuers, at $23.5 billion and $19.8 billion, respectively, recording over 40 percent increases when compared to 2024. Argentina ($9.8 billion) and Peru ($6.4 billion) also tapped international bond markets in 2025, recording increases of almost double and 64.5 percent, respectively, above the previous year, whereas Mexico’s new bond issuance ($8.2 billion) remained almost unchanged from 2024. 19

text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 New disbursements to LMICs’ PNG sectors from commercial banks and other private creditors, the other component of PNG flows, increased 27.0 percent to a record $594.6 billion in 2025. The volume of these new disbursements was dominated by China and Brazil, which accounted for a 20.1 percent and 17.7 percent share, respectively. Both countries’ debt portfolios are heavily concentrated on borrowing from this creditor group, and both recorded the highest principal repayments on these obligations. LMICs’ principal repayments on PNG borrowing from commercial banks and other private creditors moderately increased in 2025, by 3.1 percent to $508.1 billion. Although China accounted for 33.9 percent of these payments among all LMICs, which increased 20.3 percent in 2025 to $172.1 billion, Brazil’s share was 15.3 percent, and its payments to this creditor group decreased 10.3 percent to $78.0 billion in 2025. The net effect of new disbursements and principal repayments on PNG net debt flows for this group of creditors resulted in a reversal from net debt outflows of $24.9 billion in 2024 to net debt inflows of $86.5 billion in 2025.

Net debt flows from official creditors to LMICs increased 7.7 percent to $83.0 billion in 2025, after an 18.2 percent decrease in 2024. As financing from the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic has continued to taper off, official creditors’ share of total long-term debt inflows decreased from 46.2 percent in 2024 to 24.8 percent in 2025. Net debt inflows from official multilateral creditors accounted for 89.4 percent of the official flows, increasing 3.8 percent to $74.1 billion in 2025. Inflows from official bilateral creditors almost doubled to $8.8 billion but accounted for a moderate 10.6 percent share of total official flows. Increased extraordinary financing from the European Union and select bilateral creditors toward the Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration Loans for Ukraine initiative raised the total official inflows of LMICs in 2025. When Ukraine is excluded, LMICs’ net debt inflows from official multilateral creditors decreased 42.4 percent to $42.7 billion in 2025.

For this group of countries, official bilateral creditors recorded a strong increase of 43.7 percent in 2025, to $5.3 billion, which remained below the $17.2 billion decade average recorded, before plummeting in 2024. Net debt flows from the World Bank Group (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development [IBRD] and IDA financing) continued to remain positive in 2025, at $20.0 billion. Unlike procyclical lending from private creditors, lending from official creditors, including multilateral institutions, is highly countercyclical in nature. During the COVID-19 pandemic and its aftermath, the World Bank Group and other multilateral institutions stepped up their financing to stabilize LMIC economies through budget support lending, especially for the most vulnerable IDA-eligible countries, as private creditors and 20

1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 market financing retrenched. The general return of economic stability among LMICs is simultaneously associated with a rebound of investor confidence, as well as a decrease in new financing from the World Bank Group and other multilateral institutions. Consequently, new disbursements from IDA and IBRD financing decreased 25.0 percent to $19.3 billion and 15.3 percent to $26.3 billion, respectively. The simultaneous increases in principal repayments to IDA financing, up 5.9 percent to $9.1 billion, and IBRD financing, up 33.9 percent to $16.5 billion, resulted in an overall decrease of 44.3 percent in LMICs’ net flows from World Bank Group financing in 2025.

Unlike World Bank Group financing, net debt flows from the IMF continued to increase for a second consecutive year in 2025, to $10.1 billion, after recording an outflow of $2.4 billion in 2023. New disbursements to LMICs from the IMF increased in 2025, by 4.6 percent to $30.7 billion, as the institution provided new financing to select countries undergoing balance-of-payment difficulties in 2025. Argentina was the largest recipient among LMICs, accounting for over half of the new disbursements, at $14.4 billion, as the country continued to receive support for its stabilization and growth plans. The IMF provided $2.3 billion in new disbursements to Pakistan in 2025, using the arrangement under the Extended Fund Facility and the arrangement under the Resilience and Sustainability Facility to support the country’s efforts to achieve sustainable long-term growth. Bangladesh, Côte d’Ivoire, Ecuador, and the Arab Republic of Egypt were among the next largest recipients of IMF funding in 2025.

From the borrower side, net debt inflows were highly concentrated among the top 10 LMIC borrowers, excluding China. These countries are all classified as MICs and accounted for 88.1 percent of total net debt inflows to LMICs in 2025, and their total debt inflows increased drastically, more than doubling to $373.1 billion. Because China has been recording net debt outflows since 2022, this group of countries’ collective share of the total has become more substantial, increasing from an average 26.6 percent during the 2013–20 period to 94.6 percent during the last three years. The increase in the volume of flows and their composition varied significantly at the individual country level. Brazil, India, and Türkiye accounted for 83.0 percent of LMICs’ net long-term debt inflows to PNG borrowers; and Argentina, Mexico, and Ukraine claimed 40.3 percent of the comparable flows to public sector borrowers. Brazil and South Africa recorded the largest increases in net short-term debt inflows and accounted for a 47.1 percent share of LMICs’ short-term debt inflows; half of the top 10 borrowers recorded an outflow or nonmeaningful increase of short-term debt in 2025 (figure 1.6). 21

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Trends in Net Transfers on External Debt, 2015–25 LMICs’ long-term net debt transfers (disbursement minus total debt service payments) turned positive in 2025 after three consecutive years of negative volumes. Negative net transfers were recorded since 2022, during the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, indicating that LMICs’ new disbursements were lower than what they paid in interest and principal payments to service their debt obligations. In 2025, net debt transfers on long-term debt turned positive, reversing from an outflow of $118.4 billion in 2024 to an inflow of $45.4 billion (figure 1.7). The improvement was due to net transfers to PPG borrowers, which increased more than sevenfold to $49.9 billion, after turning slightly positive in 2024 to $6.6 billion. Conversely, net debt transfers to PNG borrowers continued to remain negative in 2025, albeit at an improving pace. Net transfers to PNG borrowers remained negative for the fourth consecutive year but improved considerably, from an outflow of $125.0 billion in 2024 to an outflow of $4.5 billion in 2025.

The substantial rise in new gross financing of 17.3 percent, combined with a much slower increase of 2.3 percent in debt service payments, resulted in the improvement in long-term net transfers to LMICs in 2025. This change is even more pronounced when China is excluded. Net transfers on long-term debt to LMICs excluding China reversed from an outflow of $48.5 billion to an inflow of $200.5 billion. For this group of countries, new gross financing increased at a much faster pace in 2025, at 25.2 percent to $1.1 trillion, and long-term debt service payments decreased by 2.4 percent, to $923.8 billion. 22

When the total prepaid or buyback amount of $34.5 billion in principal repayments is removed from these payments, total debt service of LMICs decreased by a moderate 0.7 percent in 2025. From the composition standpoint, when subtracting the buyback and prepaid principal payment amounts from total debt service payments made to bondholders alone, the annual percentage increase persists but is reduced to a much smaller pace of 2.9 percent, to $328.6 billion, in 2025. Conversely, total debt service payments owed to all other creditors recorded a decrease in 2025, including official bilateral creditors (down 0.6 percent to $52.6 billion), official multilateral creditors (down 2.6 percent to $142.4 billion), and commercial banks and other private creditors (down 1.5 percent to $703.8 billion). China, the largest borrower among LMICs, accounted for 30.0 percent of the group’s total debt service payments, and recorded a 13.7 percent increase to $419.8 billion in 2025.

The country’s largest share of debt service payments, and its largest yearly increase in payments, went to private creditors, recording a 19.2 percent increase to $330.3 billion in 2025. When China is excluded, total debt service payments of LMICs decreased 2.5 percent to $979.0 billion in 2025. For this group, the increase in total debt payments to bondholders persists, recording a 4.6 percent increase to $242.3 billion in 2025, as total payments to all other creditors continued to record a decrease. However, when the buyback and prepayment operations’ amounts are considered, debt service payments from LMICs to bondholders for this group of countries also decreased by 10.3 percent, to $207.9 billion, in 2025. Principal repayments for LMICs increased 2.7 percent in 2025, to $973.3 billion. From a creditor viewpoint, principal repayments to multilateral creditors and commercial banks and other private creditors recorded decreases in 2025, those to official bilateral creditors increased 1.9 percent to $40.4 billion, and those to bondholders increased 11.9 percent to $252.5 billion in 2025.

When China and the buyback payment operations are excluded, principal repayments to bondholders decreased 19.6 percent to $122.9 billion in 2025. As global interest rates slowly decreased further in 2025, albeit at different speeds, LMICs’ burden of total interest payments on their external debt stock position remained relatively unchanged, at $425.5 billion. Interest payments due to bondholders were the only creditor category experiencing an increase, of 17.9 percent to $110.6 billion. This increase persisted even when China’s significant borrowing from this creditor group is excluded, as interest payments from LMICs excluding China to bondholders increased 7.8 percent to 85.0 billion in 2025. This increase in the burden of repayment is correlated with the increase in borrowing from this creditor group, as international investors have returned to 25

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 lending to LMICs. However, their return has also come with higher compensation for risk—that is, with higher interest rates. LMICs’ average interest rate on new external commitments from private creditors remained elevated in 2025, at 5.7 percent, almost double the rate of the equivalent from official creditor sources (figure 1.9). Average interest rates began to increase rapidly in 2022 to tame inflation and have remained elevated since then for private creditors, whose lending tends to oscillate depending on market conditions. Improved global financial conditions have supported LMICs’ restoration of access to international capital markets. Following the effective closure of the market to high-yield issuers during 2022–23, primary market activity has rebounded decisively.

In 2025, average interest rates on new commitments from official creditors decreased 0.6 percentage point to 3.0 percent, and those charged by private creditors decreased more modestly, by 0.2 percentage point to 5.7 percent. The higher concessional terms offered by official creditors included longer grace periods and longer maturities than those offered by private creditors. The average maturity on new commitments from official creditors increased by one year in 2025, and the average maturity from private creditors remained almost unchanged. The average grace period on new commitments deteriorated for private creditors, declining by 1.2 years in 2025, but it remained almost unchanged at 6.0 years for official creditors. 26

text: 1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 Increased borrowing from private creditors has affected country lending groups disproportionately and has led to a hardening of the average terms of new loan commitments to IDA-eligible countries. These countries continued to face ever-increasing average interest rates on their new commitments, with rates reaching 8.2 percent in 2025, up 0.6 percentage point (figure 1.10). Such high average rates have not been seen since 1989 for this group of countries and pose a challenge for their economic development. By contrast, IBRD borrowers have seen improvements in their average terms of new commitments, with average interest rates decreasing from 5.8 percent in 2024 to 5.5 percent in 2025. As IDA-eligible countries continued to tap international markets to issue new bonds, they needed to pay even higher interest rates to attract investors to these instruments.

Average interest rates on external commitments of IDA-eligible countries to bondholders increased 1.0 percentage point in 2025 to 9.4 percent, and remained above rates of IBRD borrowers, which experienced a decrease of 0.3 percentage point to 5.5 percent (figure 1.11). The return of international investors to IDA-eligible countries remains uneven, concentrated in the largest borrowers, and costly, as international investors have increased their search for yield. IDA borrowers have therefore absorbed global financial shocks disproportionately. The recovery of IDA-eligible countries’ issuance at yields above 8 percent implies materially higher rollover costs and could place further pressure on interest-to-revenue ratios and financing needs. For many frontier issuers, the binding constraint has consequently shifted from market access to market affordability. 27

text: 1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 Box 1.5 Early 2026 Data Show No Signs of Slowdown in LMIC Bond Market Activity Preliminary data on public and publicly guaranteed (PPG) bond issuances for the first seven and a half months of 2026 show no signs of a slowdown in the appetite of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) for external capital market financing. In fact, more than 10 countries had already surpassed their full-year 2025 PPG bond totals before 2026 reached its midpoint, and the share of bond issuances with maturities of 10 years or more rose as well. The breadth of market access expanded notably in the first months of 2026. Several countries accessed international bond markets as PPG issuers without having done so at all in 2025. For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo issued $1.25 billion across two bonds at coupons of 8.75 and 9.50 percent, among the highest sovereign coupon rates recorded in 2026 so far.

For several countries, issuance volumes through mid-August 2026 already exceeded their full-year 2025 totals. Angola issued $4.75 billion through mid-August 2026, more than double the $2.01 billion issued across all of 2025. Its weighted average coupon also rose to 9.6 percent, up from 8.6 percent in 2025. Bosnia and Herzegovina raised $1.8 billion through mid-August, versus $412 million for all of 2025. India more than doubled its full-year 2025 PPG bond total of $1.0 billion by mid-August 2026, raising $2.5 billion. Indonesia and the Philippines also surpassed their respective 2025 full-year totals. Borrowing costs for the most vulnerable economies remained elevated and, in several cases, rose further. For Sub-Saharan African issuers specifically, the weighted average coupon on PPG bonds rose from 8.0 percent in 2025 to 8.8 percent through mid-August 2026, and the average maturity on new Sub-Saharan African PPG bonds shortened from 10.4 years in 2025 to 8.9 years, a simultaneous deterioration in both the cost and the tenor of market access.

Across the broader LMIC universe, maturities lengthened compared with 2025, reflecting a shift toward longer-tenor issuances among major borrowers. Bonds with maturities of 10 years or more accounted for 41.5 percent of total PPG issuance volume through mid-August 2026, up from 36.1 percent across all of 2025. Several major issuers, including Brazil, Mexico, and Türkiye, issued across multiple maturity tranches in a single transaction, a structure that allows borrowers to simultaneously refinance near-term obligations and extend their debt profiles. This maturity extension has unfolded against a backdrop of elevated global borrowing costs. Through mid-2026, benchmark government bond yields in major advanced economies reached multiyear highs, reflecting persistent inflationary pressures, rising public debt issuance volumes across advanced economies, and a prolonged period of restrictive monetary policy. For LMIC sovereigns, new bond (Box continues on next page) 29

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Box 1.5 Early 2026 Data Show No Signs of Slowdown in LMIC Bond Market Activity (continued) issuances are priced at a spread above these advanced economy benchmarks, meaning that structurally higher reference rates feed through directly into the total cost of new market borrowing. In this environment, 2026 has seen another year of large-scale liability management operations, with new issuance used to buy back existing bonds maturing in the near term, a pattern that helps smooth redemption profiles but does not significantly reduce the underlying stock of debt. Countries entering this environment with elevated debt stocks, limited fiscal space, and near-term maturities face the prospect of having to refinance obligations originally contracted at significantly lower rates, adding to already-strained debt service burdens.

Taken together, early 2026 PPG bond data suggest that LMIC governments have maintained robust access to international capital markets, even as the cost of that access, particularly for lower-income and frontier borrowers, has climbed. The expansion in the number of countries issuing, the pace of issuance relative to 2025, and maturities for select countries all point to continued, if increasingly expensive, engagement with private creditors. For Sub-Saharan African issuers, the combination of higher coupons and shorter maturities signals a particularly adverse shift in financing conditions that compounds already-constrained fiscal positions. These dynamics reinforce the importance of transparent debt management and underscore the role that concessional financing from the World Bank Group plays in helping the most vulnerable governments avoid excessive reliance on high-cost market borrowing.

Trends in Equity and Personal Remittances Flows, 2000–25 External debt flows should be considered alongside other cross-border financing flows that shape the resources available to LMICs. These financing flows include equity flows—foreign direct investment (FDI) and portfolio equity (PE)—as well as personal remittances. Together, they provide a broader view of the changing composition of external finance and the different forms of external resources available to LMICs. Aggregate financial inflows, comprising debt and equity flows, provide an important measure of cross-border financial integration. Within the equity component, FDI captures investment associated with a lasting interest in an enterprise and PE captures nonresident purchases and sales of equity securities classified as portfolio investment. Personal remittances are considered separately because they are transfers rather than financial account flows, but they 30

1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 remain an important source of external resources for LMICs. Against this broader backdrop, FDI has become less dynamic since 2011, whereas personal remittances have continued to expand.

Net equity inflows to LMICs declined from $371 billion in 2010 to a historic low of $219 billion in 2020 before recovering to $313 billion in 2025. PE flows to LMICs, excluding China, turned negative, to –$43.0 billion, in 2008 during the recession. Throughout the era of low interest rates, from 2009 to the onset of the pandemic in 2020, foreign investors remained cautious and PE flows to LMICs, excluding China, fell steadily until 2018 and have not recovered to the 2004 level of about $21.2 billion. In 2025, PE flows remained negative at –$21.0 billion (figure 1.12). Excluding China, nonresident investors continued to withdraw more equity capital from LMICs than they committed to new portfolio investments. FDI equity inflows to LMICs, excluding China, expanded during the early 2000s and peaked in 2011 in unison with personal remittances received, which includes both personal transfers and employees’ compensation. Excluding China, LMICs received $316.6 billion in FDI and $313.3 billion in remittances in 2011. The two have been diverging since 2011. FDI was $333.5 billion in 2025, whereas personal remittances grew to $687.1 billion, more than double its 2011 level (figure 1.13).

From 2000 to 2011, average annual growth rates of both FDI and personal remittances were both 15.3 percent. From 2012 until 2022, the average annual percentage growth of FDI dropped substantially, to just 1.2 percent, whereas personal remittances grew on average 6.0 percent. 31

text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Rising debt obligations of IDA-eligible countries between 2010 and 2025 combined with subdued FDI inflows constrained the scope for investment-led long-term growth. This situation put additional pressure on the limited fiscal space available to IDA-eligible borrowers to pursue development priorities while meeting their debt service obligations.

Personal remittance flows to IDA countries grew substantially in 2025 and have outpaced the FDI those countries received over the last two decades, which has led to a large divergence between IBRD and IDA borrowers. Remittances received by IDA countries went from $11.1 billion in 2000 to $203.6 billion in 2025, whereas the amount of direct investment they received remained below its previous record of $42.9 billion in 2011 for about two decades until 2024. Investment and remittances received by IBRD borrowers, excluding China, both grew with equal momentum until 2013. FDI received by IBRD countries (excluding China) grew from $76.1 billion in 2000 to $273.8 billion in 2011. Over the next decade, however, investment in IBRD borrowers stagnated around $249.1 billion, which is the annual average investment received from 2012 to 2025 (figure 1.14). 32

1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 Key Debt Indicators, 2015–25 In 2025, LMICs’ external debt ratios remained mainly stable from the peak levels recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020; however, aggregate improvement was uneven, with debt stock ratios rising or holding flat while debt service and interest payment ratios declined across most borrower groups. This change in ratios reflects a combination of strong export and income growth, the completion of debt restructuring agreements in several IDA-eligible countries, and the depreciation of the US dollar, which inflated the dollar-measured value of both debt stocks and GNI simultaneously through an accounting effect, partly moderating ratio movements in both directions. Ratios of debt to national income and exports are valuable indicators of countries’ ability to service their debt. For LMICs excluding China, the external debt-to-GNI ratio increased from 33.5 percent in 2024 to 34.5 percent in 2025, as the rise in debt stock of 9.1 percent exceeded GNI growth of 6.0 percent in 2025.

The external debt stock of the group reached $7.2 trillion in 2025, an increase of 56.4 percent compared to 2015, reflecting a decade of external borrowing that has increased the debt burden in absolute terms. LMICs excluding China improved in the overall debt service-to-GNI ratio, from 5.1 percent in 2024 to 4.7 percent in 2025, with total debt service declining from $1 trillion to $979 billion. Moreover, interest payments also declined modestly, with the interest payment-to-GNI ratio declining from 1.5 in 2024 to 1.4 percent in 2025.

The external debt-to-GNI ratio in IDA-eligible countries declined from 42.1 percent in 2024 to 41.2 percent in 2025, an improvement after two consecutive years of increases that took the ratio from 30.5 percent in 2015 to its peak in 2024 (figure 1.16). This improvement was driven by GNI growth of 10.5 percent that outpaced the 8.1 percent increase in debt stock. The debt service-to-GNI and interest-to-GNI ratios for IDA-eligible countries declined from 4.2 percent and 1.4 percent in 2024 to 3.7 percent and 1.3 percent, respectively, in 2025, reflecting a 2.3 percent decrease in total debt service obligations and stable interest payments. Similarly, LICs recorded a marginal deterioration in their external debt-to-GNI ratio, which rose from 41.1 percent in 2024 to 42.3 percent in 2025, as debt stock growth outpaced income growth; the debt service-to-GNI ratio remained broadly stable at approximately 2.0 percent in both years. The interest-to-GNI ratio also improved slightly, from 1.1 percent in 2024 to 1.0 percent in 2025, supported by income growth outpacing flat interest payments of $6.0 billion.
Yet interest costs for this group have grown at nearly double the annual average rate recorded over the 2015–25 period, reflecting the structural rise in borrowing costs in recent years. 35

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 The 2025 data point to a range of outcomes for the group and regions, with a few recording distinct trends. Sub-Saharan Africa continued to carry one of the heaviest debt burdens relative to income, with the debt-to-GNI ratio at 48.0 percent, well above the 34.4 percent recorded in 2015 and equivalent to nearly half of the region’s annual national income. Debt service and interest payments relative to GNI, at 4.4 and 1.6 percent, respectively, remained among the highest recorded for the region over the decade, but both ratios are partly weighted by South Africa’s contribution to the regional aggregate. Europe and Central Asia retained the highest debt service-to-GNI and interest-to-GNI ratios among all LMIC regions in 2025, at 7.9 and 2.2 percent respectively; however, the debt service-to-GNI ratio declined slightly from 8.1 percent in 2024, and the interest-to-GNI ratio remained stable.

The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region recorded the largest single-year increase in its debt-to-GNI ratio of any region, rising from 26.7 to 29.4 percent, signaling continued stock accumulation even as its debt service ratios improved by 0.4 percentage point in 2025 to 3.1 percent. Relative to export earnings, which reflect a country’s capacity to generate the foreign currency needed to meet external obligations, the picture is similar. For LMICs excluding China, the external debt-to-exports ratio increased from 113.0 percent in 2024 to 114.9 percent in 2025 but remains approximately 15.6 percentage points below the decade average, reflecting an overall improvement since 2015, driven by export growth rather than debt reduction (figure 1.17). text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Trends in External Debt of IDA-Eligible Countries, 2015–25 External debt stock of IDA-eligible countries reached a record $1.3 trillion in 2025, accumulating at a rate of 8.1 percent, faster than that of the other LMICs. The pace of accumulation was much higher than the 2.9 percent average recorded during the past three years and raises sustainability concerns for this group of countries. Long-term debt stock rose by 7.9 percent, and short-term debt rose by 10.7 percent, bringing the end-2025 external debt stock to almost double the 2015 level. Long-term obligations of the PPG sector grew at a faster rate of 9.0 percent than the 4.3 percent increase of the PNG debt stock. As a share, PPG debt represented 76.3 percent of total long-term obligations of IDA-eligible countries, remaining almost unchanged from 2024 and 10 percent higher than in 2015. Debt stock owed to official creditors increased 8.1 percent to $722.1 billion in 2025, representing 80.8 percent of long-term PPG debt. Obligations owed to this creditor group have remained stable over the past decade, but the composition has slightly changed over this period.

In 2025, debt stock owed to official bilateral creditors increased 2.7 percent in 2025, to $241.5 billion, and debt stock owed to multilateral creditors also increased, by 11.0 percent to $480.6 billion (figure 1.18). Multilateral creditors continued to be the most significant creditors for IDA-eligible countries, on average, accounting for half of the official debt position and up 7 percentage points from a decade ago. Debt owed to other private creditors increased 4.8 percent to $333.1 billion.

Despite facing already-elevated indebtedness levels, net debt inflows to IDA-eligible countries increased 29.0 percent in 2025, to $66.9 billion (table 1.2). About 80 percent of these inflows were long-term debt inflows, which rose 12.2 percent to $54.2 billion and registered a noted change in creditor composition. Short-term debt inflows also increased, almost quadrupling to $12.7 billion. The increase in long-term debt flows was driven by private creditor entities, whose net debt inflows in 2025 doubled to $23.9 billion. During the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, private creditors contracted in 2022 and remained below the prepandemic trends during 2023 and 2024; multilateral institutions stepped in to provide emergency financing for countries affected by the crisis. text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 2025, increasing 10.5 percent to $3.2 trillion, the pandemic era financing patterns reversed, recording an increase in inflows from private creditors and a simultaneous decrease in inflows from official creditors. The increase in net debt flows from private creditors occurred because of a combined increase in net debt flows from bondholders and from banks and other private creditors. Net debt flows from bondholders increased 73.6 percent in 2025, to $13.5 billion, and were mostly concentrated in borrowing by the public sector, which increased 57.4 percent to $11.9 billion. Net debt inflows from banks and other private creditors more than tripled to $10.4 billion in 2025. The increase was led by net flows to PNG borrowers, which account for a bigger share of the total and switched from an outflow of $572.1 million in 2024 to an inflow of $8.3 billion in 2025. Conversely, net flows from public sector borrowers to this creditor group decreased 36.5 percent to $2.1 billion.

The restoration of access to capital markets has been particularly consequential for Sub-Saharan Africa, which accounted for 64 percent of IDA-eligible countries’ total public sector issuances (figure 1.19). The public sectors of eight countries in Sub-Saharan Africa collectively raised approximately $11.8 billion by end-December 2025, a marked 36.2 percent increase over 2024. Several issuers returned after prolonged absences: Kenya, the largest issuer in the region, raised $3.5 billion in 2025. The country returned to bond markets to prepay its 2027 and 2028 maturity obligations ahead of schedule. Côte d’Ivoire raised a total of $2.5 billion in 2025. Importantly, a substantial share of proceeds from the two countries’ debt offerings funded their liability management operations, refinancing upcoming bullet maturities, and thereby easing rollover pressures. Nigeria, the third-largest issuer in the region, raised $2.3 billion in a dual-tranche international bond issue that was divided into one tranche with a 10-year maturity at 8.625 percent and a second, 20-year maturity tranche at 9.125 percent.

Remarkably, Uganda’s share of domestic currency government debt held by nonresidents reached $2.8 billion in 2025, indicating strong demand for high-yield debt from international investors. Among countries in other regions, Uzbekistan recorded the highest international bond issuance among IDA-eligible countries in 2025, at $3.9 billion. The public sector issuance was divided between $1.6 billion in issuances from the general government sector, including issuances in domestic currency, and $2.4 billion in issuances from other public sector entities. Suriname completed its first international issuance since 2016. 40

The restoration of access to capital markets has come at a higher cost for public sector entities in IDA-eligible countries, however. Although the average interest rate on new commitments from official creditors has remained relatively steady at 2.7 percent over the 2024–25 period, the average rate on new commitments from private creditors continued to increase in 2025, to 8.2 percent, up 0.6 percentage point from 2024. Such elevated interest rates have not been seen since 1989 for public sector entities in this group of countries, when rates spiked in reaction to the 1980s debt crisis. Overall, IDA-eligible countries, which can borrow on highly concessional terms, paid an average 5.5 percentage points higher interest rate in 2025 when borrowing from private creditors than from official ones.
