text: 1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 After hitting an all-time high in 2024, the cost of servicing IDA-eligible countries’ external debt obligations (interest plus principal repayments) decreased 2.3 percent in 2025, to $117.2 billion. The decrease in total debt servicing cost was due to a 2.9 percent decrease in principal repayments on total external debt, to $77.6 billion, which accounted for a 66 percent share of the total payments made by this group of countries in 2025. Interest payments on total liabilities also decreased, by 1.2 percent, to $39.6 billion in 2025, after recording a record high volume of $40.1 billion in 2024. From a debtor’s viewpoint, the decrease was led by PNG sector borrowing, which fell 9.5 percent to $40.9 billion, but the cost of servicing public sector debt continued to increase, by 2.5 percent, in 2025 to $71.3 billion. Debt service payments on PPG debt have been on the rise for five consecutive years since 2020 and marked another record high for IDA-eligible countries in 2025.

The increase continues to limit these countries’ fiscal space and raises sustainability concerns for this group, which is eligible to borrow on concessional terms from IDA to support countries’ debt sustainability and includes some of the poorest countries.

Debt service payments from PPG borrowers to multilateral institutions and private creditors were the main drivers of the increase in total PPG debt service costs. Debt service payments to multilateral institutions increased 3.6 percent, to $30.6 billion, and accounted for 42.9 percent of PPG borrowers’ total payments. IDA-eligible countries owe more than half of their public sector debt to this group of creditors because of the concessional terms these institutions typically provide. Notably, as principal payments made to this creditor base increased 7.6 percent in 2025, to $20.3 billion, interest payments decreased 3.5 percent to $10.3 billion. Debt service payments made by public sector entities to bondholders increased at a much faster pace of 16.9 percent, to $13.1 billion. Bondholders accounted for 18.4 percent of the debt service payments to PPG creditors, an increase of 8 percentage points since 2023. This share has been increasing over the past two years, whereas the respective share in debt stock position has remained stable over the decade at an average of 12 percent.

Principal repayments made to this creditor group increased 5.8 percent in 2025, to $6.6 billion, and included advance repayments from buyback operations made by Kenya and Suriname. Interest payments increased at a much faster pace of 30.7 percent in 2025, to $6.5 billion. These costs are projected to increase as IDA-eligible countries continue to tap international markets at an accelerated pace, amid an environment of elevated global interest rates. Among IDA-eligible countries, net debt transfers to PPG borrowers decreased 20.3 percent, to $20.1 billion in 2025. The overall decrease in new disbursements by 9.6 percent to $63.7 billion led to a decrease in official net transfers to PPG borrowers of IDA-eligible countries in 2025, as debt service payments remained 43

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 relatively flat at $48.6 billion. Net transfers from official creditors remained positive at $15.1 billion but decreased 29.8 percent from the previous year (figure 1.21), the second consecutive yearly decrease. Conversely, net transfers from private creditors to PPG borrowers increased 36.7 percent to $4.9 billion in 2025, following a reversal from a net outflow of $2.8 billion in 2023 to a net inflow of $3.6 billion in 2024. The increase in 2025 was driven by a 14.2 percent increase in new disbursements from this creditor base, which increased at a much faster pace than total debt service payments.

Debt Reorganization, 2025 The total amount of debt reorganization fell markedly in 2025 from the record $90 billion in 2024. Moreover, it was characterized by two very different types of operations and accompanied by a shift in emphasis to MICs. The first and most significant element of debt reorganization in 2025 was large-scale sovereign bond buyback and exchange operations initiated by governments in middle-income and, to a lesser degree, IDA-eligible countries, and financed by new sovereign bond issuance. These liability management operations, all undertaken on a voluntary basis, aimed primarily to meet financing needs and enhance the public debt portfolio. text: 1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 centered on IDA-eligible countries and the implementation of the debt restructuring agreed to in the memorandum of understanding (MoU) by the Group of Twenty (G-20) Common Framework for Ghana and Zambia, signed in December 2023 and June 2024, respectively, and with Sri Lanka, conducted outside the Common Framework, also signed in June 2024. There were no new requests from debtor countries for a debt treatment in the Common Framework or the Paris Club in 2025.

Efforts to enhance the debt restructuring architecture continued in 2025 primarily through reforms to the G-20 Common Framework, facilitated by the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable. Since its creation in 2020, the G-20 Common Framework has served as the coordinating mechanism for the provision of comprehensive debt restructuring for IDA-eligible countries. It brings together all G-20 bilateral creditors and coordinates with private creditor groups to provide a debt treatment, tailored to each borrower’s debt structure, to restore medium-term debt sustainability. A key area of progress in 2025 was the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable endorsement of early publication by the debtor of the key debt restructuring parameters, namely (a) the net present value reduction; (b) the reduction in debt service over the IMF program period; and (c) the change in the duration of treated claims. This information provides private creditors with an up-front indicator of comparability of treatment requirements.

A new MoU Implementation Table was also introduced as a monitoring tool to track the status of agreements with each bilateral creditor signatory to the MoU, and with the expectation that these agreements would be finalized within 12 months of the signing of the MoU.3 The London Coalition, the coordinating body for restructuring by private creditors, developed an Implementation Guide to Restructuring Private Sector Sovereign Loans, and the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable updated the restructuring guidelines to reflect the latest common understandings. The transparency agenda could have been advanced by disclosure of the amount covered by each agreement. Currently, only a handful of G-20 bilateral creditors publish information on the amount and terms of rescheduling agreements on official websites.

Debt Restructuring in 2025 Debt restructuring in 2025 focused on implementation of an MoU between bilateral creditors and Ghana, Sri Lanka, and Zambia. As discussed in detail in International Debt Report 2025, all three countries finalized and concluded a restructuring agreement with bondholders in 2024. The pace of implementation of bilateral agreements accelerated in 2025, and, after long and protracted negotiations, an MoU was also signed with Ethiopia. 45

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Ghana signed an MoU with 25 bilateral creditors in 2024 to restructure about $5.4 billion in outstanding debt. The agreement consolidated $2.8 billion in principal and interest due from December 2022 to end-December 2026 into a new loan with a 15-year grace period and repayable between 2039 and 2043, with interest rates capped at 3 percent. The agreement delivered a 37 percent reduction in net present value. By end-2025, Ghana had signed a bilateral agreement with 7 of the 25 creditors that signed the MoU, including, in order of the date of signature, France, China, Finland, the United Kingdom, Spain, Germany, and Czechia. The amount restructured by these agreements has not been disclosed, and the restructuring was not reflected in the 2025 debt data reported to the Debtor Reporting System.

Sri Lanka signed an MoU with 17 creditors in June 2024 to restructure $5.8 billion and a parallel agreement with the Export-Import Bank of China for $4.2 billion, bringing the overall total to $10 billion. The agreements restructured the stock of debt outstanding on January 1, 2023, and extended the maturity until 2042, with a five-year grace period. By end-2025, Sri Lanka had signed a bilateral agreement with 7 of the 17 creditors that signed the MoU, including, in order of the date of signature, Japan, India, France, Hungary, Australia, and Denmark, and the agreement with China. Together, these creditors restructured $8.8 billion, equivalent to 88 percent of the $10 billion agreed to. In addition, an agreement to restructure $2.2 billion owed to the China Development Bank on terms comparable to those accorded by international bondholders was also signed. Zambia signed an MoU with 16 bilateral creditors in December 2023 that restructured about $6.3 billion in outstanding debt. The agreement extended maturities by 12 years and pushed average maturities to beyond 20 years.

Interest rates were reduced according to a structured schedule and set at 1.0 percent for the first 14 years, gradually increasing thereafter to a maximum of 2.5 percent. The revised terms provided significant debt relief. Over the next decade, Zambia will make debt service payments of about $750 million, compared to nearly $6 billion originally due. By end-2025 Zambia had signed a bilateral agreement with 6 of the 16 creditors signatory to the MoU, including, in order of the date of signature, Saudi Arabia, France, China, India, the United Kingdom, and Japan. Based on information reported to the Debtor Reporting System, together these creditors restructured $3.9 billion, equivalent to about 62 percent of the total of $6.3 billion agreed to by bilateral creditors in the MoU. Ethiopia concluded negotiations with bilateral creditors in 2025. It reached an agreement in principle with the Official Creditor Committee in March 2025, and an MoU covering approximately $8.4 billion was signed by all 14 Official Creditor Committee members in December 2025. The first bilateral agreement 46

1. ANALysIs Of ExTERNAL DEBT sTOcks AND DEBT fLOws As Of END-2025 with France was signed in February 2026. Regarding the restructuring with bondholders, an initial agreement was rejected by bilateral creditors on the grounds that it fell short of comparability-of-treatment requirements. A revised proposal was subsequently endorsed by bilateral creditors in August 2026, and an agreement with bondholders is expected to be signed and implemented by the end of 2026.

Other than the countries discussed in the preceding paragraphs, debt restructuring in 2025 was limited. The most significant operation was the bilateral agreement between China and Kenya to reschedule the terms of $3.5 billion in loans extended for construction of the Mombasa-Naivasha Railway. The agreement increased the grace period and extended the maturity by five years. It also swapped the currency in which the loans are repayable from US dollars to Chinese yuan with a concomitant conversion of the interest rate from the Federal Reserve Secure Overnight Financing Rate to China’s yuan-denominated Loan Prime Rate. In Pakistan, the Chinese government extended the maturities on agreements under which approximately $2 billion is due in 2025. Liability Management Operations in 2025 Tenders by LMICs to buy back or exchange sovereign bonds increased markedly in 2025 as governments used new bond issuance to refinance existing obligations and actively manage their debt portfolios. Based on data reported to the Debtor Reporting System, 14 countries repurchased $34.5 billion in outstanding sovereign bonds in 2025, with the largest operations concentrated in MICs (figure 1.22).

Although the scale and structure of these transactions varied, both middle-income and IDA-eligible countries sought to reduce near-term refinancing pressures, extend maturity profiles, manage currency and interest rate exposure, and, in some cases, support state-owned enterprises. The select country cases discussed in the following paragraphs—Mexico, the Dominican Republic, Kenya, and Côte d’Ivoire—illustrate the range of approaches and outcomes observed during the year. Mexico. In 2025, the government of Mexico conducted a series of coordinated liability-management operations to ease near-term refinancing pressures and provide financial support to Petróleos Mexicanos (PEMEX), the state-owned petroleum company. In June 2025, the government issued $6.80 billion in two global bonds: a $3.95 billion, 5.850 percent note due in 2032; and a $2.85 billion, 6.625 percent note due in 2038. Part of the proceeds financed the early repurchase of the $2.06 billion outstanding on a 4.125 percent note due in January 2026. The government also exchanged $2.5 billion outstanding on a series of nine 47

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 dollar-denominated bonds maturing between 2027 and 2031 for the newly issued securities. Strong investor participation in the exchange operation realized a 15 percent reduction, equivalent to $207 million, in outstanding US dollar– denominated bonds due in 2027–31. In August 2025, the government also redeemed in full the €1.33 billion outstanding on its 1.625 percent global notes due in 2026.

In September 2025, the government issued $8.0 billion and €5.0 billion in multitranche sovereign bonds. The US dollar issuance comprised $1.5 billion of 4.750 percent notes due in 2031, $4.0 billion of 5.375 percent notes due in 2033, and $2.5 billion of 5.625 percent notes due in 2035. The euro issuance comprised €2.50 billion of 3.500 percent notes due in 2029, €1.50 billion of 4.500 percent notes due in 2034, and €1.25 billion of 5.125 percent notes due in 2038. These transactions enabled a capital contribution of nearly $14 billion from the federal government to PEMEX, which in turn used the funds to partially repay and redeem short-term securities maturing in 2025 and to finance a $9.9 billion multiseries bond buyback targeting maturities from 2026 to 2028. The operation smoothed PEMEX’s debt-maturity profile and improved its liquidity but largely transferred debt service risk to the sovereign rather than materially reducing consolidated public sector liabilities. 48

The new issuance comprised three tranches: a $2 billion, 6.95 percent global note due in 2037; a $1 billion, 7.15 percent global note due in 2055; and a tranche indexed to the Dominican peso (RD$) of RD$125 billion at 10.50 percent, due in 2037. By combining new issuance with debt repurchases, the government reduced its exposure to foreign currency debt, extended the average maturity of its global bonds, and lowered financing needs for 2026.

Kenya. In March 2025, the government of Kenya issued a $1.5 billion Eurobond at 9.5 percent, due in 2036. A part of the proceeds was used to repurchase approximately $579.7 million of the outstanding $900 million, 7 percent Eurobond due in 2027. In October 2025, the government of Kenya raised a further $1.5 billion through a dual-tranche Eurobond issuance, comprising two equal $750 million tranches: a 7.875 percent note due in 2033 and an 8.80 percent note due in 2038. This measure marked Kenya’s second major liability-management operation in less than two years and aimed to extend maturities and reduce refinancing costs. The proceeds were used to repurchase approximately $628.4 million of the outstanding $1.0 billion, 7.250 percent notes due in 2028. The 2025 buyback operation extended debt maturities and eased near-term refinancing pressures but largely functioned as a refinancing maneuver rather than reducing the overall debt stock.

Côte d’Ivoire. In March 2025, Côte d’Ivoire issued a $1.75 billion, 8.075 percent Eurobond due in 2036. Part of the proceeds financed the repurchase of two earlier-maturing bonds: a US dollar–denominated 6.375 percent note due in 2028, and a euro-denominated 4.875 percent note due in 2032. 2. Debt Dynamics: Policy Implications External Debt, External Shocks, and Vulnerability in LMICs Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) are facing historically high global uncertainty at a time when external debt stocks have reached historic highs, debt service pressures remain elevated, fiscal space is limited in many countries, and global bond yields continue to rise, tightening financial conditions. This combination matters because external shocks can be more difficult to absorb when governments already face substantial financing needs and limited room to respond. The key vulnerability therefore lies not in exposure to global shocks alone but in how those shocks interact with already-high debt burdens. Adverse developments in trade, commodity markets, growth, exchange rates, and tighter global financing conditions all have the potential to weaken external and fiscal positions, and high debt levels can amplify their economic and development consequences and impair the effectiveness of policy responses. International Debt Report 2025 documented the scale of external debt burdens and their links to economic growth and vulnerability (World Bank 2025).

Building on that assessment, this year’s report focuses on the interactions between external shocks and external debt burdens, and how debt might amplify vulnerabilities when global conditions deteriorate. This chapter examines the channels through which these interactions operate across LMICs. The chapter further discusses how rising debt service burdens, elevated financing needs, and changing financing patterns are constraining fiscal space and intensifying debt and rollover risks, as well as the policy priorities for strengthening resilience. Finally, food and nutrition security provides a concrete example of these interactions, illustrating how debt burdens may be closely associated with a decline in the affordability of a healthy diet during periods of global stress. Global uncertainty rose sharply in 2025 (figure 2.1) and remained elevated into 2026. The World Uncertainty Index measures broad uncertainty and rose more than fivefold between the third quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2025, nearly twice its COVID-19 peak. The Global Economic Policy Uncertainty Index showed a similar pattern, rising sharply in early 2025 and remaining elevated into 2026 (Ahir et al.

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Elevated uncertainty matters because economies remain closely connected to international markets. Yet countries differ in the nature and degree of their external exposure, which shapes how global external shocks affect them. Trade provides an important example. As figure 2.2 shows, global imports and exports of goods and services increased from below 25 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the early 2000s, were halted by the 2008 global financial crisis, and subsequently rebounded and have fluctuated around 30 percent. Exposure, however, varies significantly across income groups. In 2025, imports accounted for about 34 percent of GDP in low-income economies, compared with exports of about 24 percent; trade flows were much more balanced in high-income economies. The next section discusses these transmission channels in greater detail, including the roles of trade and financial exposure, exchange rates, inflation, and policy buffers, and how external debt can amplify vulnerabilities when shocks occur. 52

text: 2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs Transmission of External Shocks External shocks are transmitted to LMICs differently, depending on their structural features. Economies that rely heavily on imports of goods and services for domestic activity are vulnerable to sudden changes in the external environment, such as production shortfalls in major supplier countries, export restrictions, or supply chain disruptions; in contrast, export-oriented economies are more vulnerable to shifts in demand among their trading partners. External shocks also tend to spill more forcefully into LMICs with open financial markets, partly reflecting rapid capital flow movements. In addition, the types of policy frameworks in LMICs are important for the transmission of external shocks. For example, in economies with flexible exchange rate regimes, the effects of external shocks are partly absorbed through currency movements. In economies with fixed exchange rate regimes, pressure on the exchange rate can be cushioned by using foreign reserves.

As discussed later in this chapter, damage from external shocks that LMICs can absorb and the speed of subsequent recovery are also subject to the availability of fiscal buffers and the implementation of fiscal and foreign exchange policy frameworks. 53

text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 External debt is a key amplifier of the transmission of external shocks. Economies with elevated external debt levels, especially short-term debt, are vulnerable to sudden shifts in investor risk appetite and rollover risks, potentially leading to sudden stops in capital flows and current account reversals. For most LMICs, where external debt tends to be denominated in foreign currencies, economic vulnerabilities can increase when external shocks lead to currency depreciation, causing an increase in debt service burdens and higher inflation. An increase in debt service costs can slow investment growth by decreasing national savings. During periods of tightening global financial conditions, LMICs with high levels of external debt need to raise interest rates to defend their currencies, causing credit crunches in domestic financial markets and slowing growth. Despite a recent slowdown in international integration, LMICs have become more exposed to external shocks, while also accumulating external debt.

In LMICs, although the pace of trade integration has slowed, trade openness, measured as the sum of exports and imports as a share of GDP, increased to about 48 percent in 2025, up from about 44 percent in the mid-2010s (figure 2.3). An increase in trade openness is broad based across LMICs, with more than 60 percent of economies experiencing an increase between 54

text: 2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs 2015–19 and 2020–25. Financial openness, represented by the sum of foreign assets and liabilities as a share of GDP, remained nearly unchanged from the mid-2010s through 2024. International financial integration has slowed since the pandemic in 2020, but that slowdown has been driven primarily by major economies; financial openness increased in almost 70 percent of LMICs between 2015–19 and 2020–24. In addition, as presented in chapter 1, external debt stocks in LMICs rose to $9.4 trillion by the end of 2025, an increase of $3.5 trillion since 2015.

The nature of external shocks also affects the different degrees of shock transmission to LMICs. For example, global supply shocks, including shortages of energy, food, and other commodities—and rapid increases in their prices, which tend to be caused by wars and conflicts as well as extreme weather-related events—have a larger impact on commodity importers. The outbreak of a conflict involving major commodity producers can halt their exports, and the impact can be exacerbated by logistical disruptions such as port or shipping lane closures. Particularly in food-producing economies, disasters associated with extreme weather, including storms and droughts potentially caused by El Niño, can decrease global food production and disrupt global trade. In addition, abrupt shifts in trade policies, including the imposition of tariffs or export bans, can restrict access to key commodities. In contrast, commodity exporters tend to be affected more by adverse global demand shocks, including slowdowns in global activity triggered by major systemic events such as financial crises and pandemic-driven lockdowns, and the resulting plunges in commodity prices.

In commodity-importing LMICs, external shocks can be transmitted through multiple channels. Higher global energy and food prices, along with disruptions to shipping and global value chains, raise production and transportation costs. The resulting rise in domestic inflation in these economies drives up the cost of living, with disproportionate effects on poorer economies and households, where food accounts for a larger share of consumption. The purchasing power of consumers declines as real incomes fall, resulting in reduced spending. In addition, higher prices of commodities and other imported materials increase overall import costs, worsening terms of trade and current account balances. Financial conditions can tighten because of hikes in interest rates to combat increased inflation, raising borrowing costs. Pressures of currency depreciation rise, increasing the costs of servicing debt denominated in foreign currencies. Fiscal positions deteriorate, with increasing spending pressures, including fuel and food subsidies, and slower activity can lower revenue collection. 55

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Inflation in commodity-importing LMICs has increased following a major energy supply shock in 2026. The conflict in the Middle East involving major energy producers, which began at the end of February 2026, has caused a surge in headline inflation in these countries, to 3.6 percent in June 2026, from the preconflict level of 2.6 percent (figure 2.4). Among market participants, inflation expectations for 2026 have also risen, from 2.7 percent according to preconflict February surveys to 3.4 percent in July. Excluding China, which has been relatively insulated from the shock, partly because of its large petroleum reserves, inflation in commodity-importing LMICs increased from 7.0 percent to 8.3 percent between January and June, with higher inflation expectations for 2026. Energy prices have increased, as well, by 1.1 percentage points between January and June 2026 (excluding China). To ease price pressures, several central banks have raised interest rates. In addition, several commodity-importing LMICs have introduced subsidies in response to higher fuel prices (World Bank 2026b). 56

text: 2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs The energy supply shock in 2026 has caused exchange rates in commodity-importing LMICs to fall, worsening trade balances. Among commodity-importing LMICs with flexible or adjustable exchange rate regimes, currencies depreciated by about 1.7 percent between January and July 2026 (figure 2.5), on average. In contrast, currencies in commodity-exporting LMICs with flexible regimes appreciated by an average of 2.5 percent over the same period. Currency pressures have made imports more expensive in commodity importers and worsened trade balances. Across commodity-importing LMICs with flexible or adjustable currency regimes, merchandise import values, in US dollar terms, increased by an average 23 percent between February and June 2026 compared with the same months of 2025. Excluding China, the rate of increase was 21 percent, on average. As import values increased faster than those of exports, merchandise trade deficits—without China—expanded in the first half of 2026. Between February and June 2026, merchandise trade deficits averaged almost $20 billion higher than in the same months of the previous year. 57

text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Global demand shocks affect commodity-exporting LMICs directly and indirectly. Collapses in global commodity prices directly reduce export earnings and profits in the commodity-related sector, reducing domestic demand and activity. Revenue declines cause deterioration of fiscal positions and the debt service mechanism, while also leading to worsening terms of trade and current account balances. With reduced debt repayment capacity, sovereign risk premiums increase, raising debt refinancing costs, eroding investor confidence, and potentially triggering sudden capital outflows. Financial conditions are tightened, with lower credit availability and a weakened banking sector, along with a rise in nonperforming loans. Declines in foreign exchange earnings also lead to currency depreciation, which increases inflationary pressure and living costs.

The impact of external shocks tends to be larger and more persistent in fragile economies and low-income countries (LICs). In both LICs and economies in fragile, conflict, and violence-affected environments or with institutional fragility, financial markets tend to be shallower than in other LMICs, making them more exposed to external shocks. They tend to rely on narrower economic bases, in terms of exports and revenue sources, and are therefore more affected by sudden shifts in external conditions. With a weak institutional framework and limited access to financing, these economies tend to implement procyclical fiscal tightening during economic downturns. Increases in commodity prices and supply shortages translate into substantial losses in economic welfare and income, reflecting persistently low personal savings and acute food insecurity. International reserves and credible monetary policies can help cushion the adverse impact of external shocks in LMICs. The accumulation of foreign exchange reserves can defend against sharp currency depreciation and can be used to pay for imports of commodities and other essential products.

LMICs have increased their foreign exchange reserves over the past decade, reaching more than $6 trillion at the end of June 2026. Excluding China, foreign exchange increased to $2.6 trillion in June. However, the pace of foreign exchange accumulation has slowed since March 2026, particularly in commodity-importing LMICs, mainly because of the conflict in the Middle East (figure 2.6). Facing a rise in import costs driven by currency depreciation, some of these economies have been forced to draw on their reserves. This trend has been exacerbated by outflows of foreign currency, mainly driven by rising global risk aversion. In addition, credible monetary policy frameworks act as critical policy buffers against external shocks in LMICs. They help anchor long-term inflation expectations and reduce the transmission of global shocks, such as commodity price changes and financial market volatility, to domestic inflation. Preconditions for the effectiveness of the frameworks include greater independence for central banks and transparent communication of monetary policy. 58

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs Robust fiscal policy frameworks can also act as strong policy buffers against external shocks. Fiscal rules help manage revenue volatility and excess spending during booms; stabilization funds, especially in commodity-exporting LMICs, can mitigate the procyclicality of fiscal policy by saving revenues during booms and deploying them when commodity prices and revenues collapse. Since 2000, many commodity-exporting LMICs have adopted such frameworks (figure 2.7). However, successful implementation requires strong institutions, including transparency and technical capacity (Vasishtha 2026). Policy priorities differ across LMICs, depending on the strength of institutional capacity and fiscal space. Economies with weaker capacity need to strengthen tax revenue mobilization and improve fiscal transparency. 59

text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Debt Sustainability and Fiscal Pressures External shocks have compounded preexisting fiscal pressures and increased debt vulnerabilities in LMICs. These countries require substantial investment to raise productivity, create jobs, and advance broader development objectives. Financing these needs depends on mobilizing domestic resources, attracting domestic and foreign private capital, and, where necessary, borrowing through public channels. In this context, part of the increase in public debt reflects efforts to finance infrastructure, human capital, and other investments that can support long-term growth. However, slower global growth, policy uncertainty, trade fragmentation, geopolitical tensions, and commodity-price volatility have affected both the availability and cost of financing. In many countries, shocks that initially generated temporary financing needs have contributed to persistently higher debt stocks, debt service burdens, and rollover requirements.

The Impact of Higher Debt on Fiscal Space and Financing Pressures The accumulation of public debt has been accompanied by a substantial increase in debt service burdens in LMICs over the past 25 years. The median total debt service in countries eligible for International Development Association (IDA) assistance increased from about 15 percent of government revenues (excluding grants) in 2000 to over 40 percent in 2025. text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 refinance maturing obligations contributes to elevated GFNs, even when fiscal deficits are narrowing. GFNs in IDA countries averaged about 6 percent of GDP during 2015–19, before increasing to roughly 10 percent during 2020–22 as pandemic-related primary deficits widened and debt service obligations increased. Subsequent shocks, including the commodity price and inflation surge following the Russian Federation’s invasion of Ukraine, and the sharp global monetary tightening that began in 2022, further contributed to elevated financing needs. GFNs subsequently moderated but remained well above their prepandemic average, at approximately 8.2 percent of GDP in 2024, before rising to 8.7 percent in 2025.

Box 2.1 The World Bank Group’s Sovereign Investor Relations Guidance Note Sovereign credit rating actions remained in flux throughout 2025. For instance, in the first half of 2025, Fitch recorded eight sovereign upgrades against four downgrades among emerging markets—a net positive trend—but revised its sector outlook for Asia-Pacific, Eastern Europe, and Sub-Saharan Africa to “deteriorating” from “neutral,” citing trade uncertainty and tightening fiscal space. Moody’s downgraded Bolivia and Botswana, while upgrading Costa Rica. This mixed picture illustrates that sovereign creditworthiness is increasingly differentiated and that the gap between countries that gain and lose market confidence is often shaped not only by fundamentals but also by how effectively governments engage with investors and creditors.

Against this backdrop, the World Bank Group has published “Sovereign Investor Relations: A Guide for Debt Managers” (Proite and Yavuz 2026), a practical handbook designed to help debt managers in low- and middle-income countries build and professionalize their investor relations functions. The guide argues that countries must move from passive disclosure to active, structured engagement that reduces information asymmetries to lower the “uncertainty premium” embedded in their borrowing costs. The guidance note covers the full spectrum of sovereign investor relations, from strategy formulation to institutional setup as well as practical tools for implementation. The guide is scalable and designed for countries at varying stages of market development, from frontier markets taking their first steps in external borrowing to frequent issuers seeking to deepen and diversify their investor bases.

The latest developments in 2026 also reinforce the core message of the guidance note—that is, in a world of differentiated sovereign credit outcomes, proactive investor relations are not a luxury but a strategic necessity. Countries that engage creditors early, communicate policy intent clearly, and manage reputational risk systematically are better positioned to preserve market access, reduce financing costs, and navigate periods of stress. 62

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs The persistence of high GFNs, despite narrower primary deficits, underscores the role of accumulated debt and higher debt service costs. Notwithstanding notable fiscal consolidation, with primary deficits in 2023–24 narrowing to approximately half their 2021–22 levels, average GFNs stabilized at about 8 percent of GDP, 2 percentage points above their prepandemic average, before increasing further in 2025. Consistent with this pattern, the distribution of debt-stabilization gaps across countries has changed little over the past 15 years (figure 2.9). These gaps, denoted as ΔDSPD, are calculated as the difference between the actual primary deficit and the debt-stabilizing primary deficit, indicating the primary deficit or surplus that would keep the debt-to-GDP ratio unchanged, given the country’s existing debt, borrowing costs, and GDP growth.2 This calculation suggests that the continued elevation of GFNs is not primarily the result of a renewed widening of primary deficits.
Rather, it reflects the debt stock accumulated following successive shocks, higher interest costs, the rollover of maturing obligations, and, in some cases, balance of payments financing needs. 63

text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Debt distress risks have eased from the deterioration observed over the past decade, particularly following the COVID-19 shock, but they remain elevated. As informed by the World Bank–International Monetary Fund Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries (LIC-DSF), the number of IDA LIC-DSF countries with unsustainable external public debt or rated as being in debt distress remains limited (at end-December 2025): out of 68 IDA LIC-DSF countries, only 11 are in debt distress or have unsustainable public debt. The share of IDA LIC-DSF countries assessed as being at high risk of external debt distress declined from a peak of 46 percent in 2021 to 35 percent in 2025. Most emerging markets remain at low or moderate risk of overall sovereign stress,3 although vulnerabilities remain uneven, and debt levels are generally above prepandemic levels. Despite these improvements, IDA LIC-DSF countries have generally moved from high to moderate risk rather than returning to their preshock levels. Between 2019 and 2025, there were a total of 37 changes in external risk (figure 2.10).

Of these changes, 22 were downgraded to higher risk of external debt distress, most of which took place after the COVID-19 shock. More recently, upgrades have reflected improved macro-fiscal conditions and, in a few cases, the completion of debt restructuring. The LIC-DSF framework underpinning these assessments has undergone a comprehensive review by the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund, with that review approved by their respective Executive Boards in September 2026. The revised framework is expected to be finalized in 2027; box 2.2 summarizes its key features. 64

text: 2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs Box 2.2 Strengthening the Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries The 2026 review of the Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group updates how the organizations assess sovereign debt risk and sustainability amid rising domestic borrowing, diversified creditor bases, and growing liquidity pressures. The revisions aim to strengthen early warning capacity and policy relevance while preserving the framework’s role in guiding borrowing and lending decisions. Key reforms include the following: • A revamped risk architecture distinguishing more clearly between external debt stress, overall public debt stress, and unsustainability • The introduction of new models for the risk of overall public debt stress and public debt unsustainability, together with an updated model for the risk of external public debt stress

• New dedicated modules to support the structured application of judgment, including – A domestic debt module to assess solvency, liquidity risk, and macro-financial linkages (including the sovereign–bank–central bank nexus); and – A long-term module to evaluate implications of policy and investment deci-sions (including climate adaptation, infrastructure, and human capital) over longer horizons • New emphasis on data quality via the new debt data confidence flag, clearer guidance on the debt perimeter, and incentives to close reporting gaps • Introduction of additional granularity to risk ratings to differentiate among countries at high risk of debt distress. The review was launched in 2024 with public consultations and stakeholder inputs gathered through 2026. The new framework is expected to become operational in the second half of 2027, allowing time to finalize the revised operational guidance and undertake extensive capacity building for users of the framework. Source: World Bank 2026c.

The Impact of Debt Composition on Liquidity and Domestic Financial Sector Risks The increase in financing needs has been accompanied by greater reliance on domestic debt. Domestic borrowing has provided an important source of financing when access to external markets is limited or costly. However, it has also increased rollover risks and strengthened the links between sovereign finances and domestic financial sector stability. 65

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Domestic creditors in both IDA and International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) countries have elevated their exposure to the sovereign over the past 20 years. This move mirrors their respective governments’ growing reliance on domestic financing. However, domestic banks in IDA countries have consistently held a greater share of their balance sheets in sovereign assets than banks in IBRD countries have (figure 2.11). This higher exposure reflects less developed and less diversified private sectors in many IDA countries, as well as fewer investment options as compared to IBRD markets. Domestic banks may therefore have few alternatives to government securities, particularly during periods of financial stress. In IDA countries, the increase in sovereign exposure goes beyond the domestic banking sector to include the central bank and the domestic nonbanking sector (figure 2.12).

Consequently, domestic debt amortization dominates GFNs for LICs, signaling mounting liquidity pressures even where sovereign solvency appears contained. These pressures reflect the short average maturity of domestic debt in most LICs and the attendant rollover burden, whereby a growing share of gross financing serves merely to refinance maturing domestic obligations. text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 borrowing increases exposure to exchange rate and refinancing shocks. At the same time, high debt limits countries’ ability to borrow to close financing gaps. Countries are therefore left increasingly exposed to shocks, with minimal fiscal and financial buffers.

Sound fiscal and debt policies are central to preparing for, responding to, and recovering from external shocks. Fiscal buffers and debt sustainability determine the extent to which countries can absorb shocks and support recovery. Countries that entered shock episodes with adequate fiscal buffers, manageable debt levels, and a track record of countercyclical policies consistently limited long-term output losses. By contrast, high debt and procyclical spending amplified the economic damage.4 The interaction of limited fiscal buffers, elevated debt vulnerabilities, and weak policy execution points to three interconnected priorities: revenue mobilization and maintaining sound debt management, adopting countercyclical fiscal strategies, and investing in fiscal institutions. Mobilizing revenue and managing debt. Revenue mobilization is not simply a matter of raising tax rates. Effective mobilization requires a holistic approach that strengthens the policy, administrative, and legal foundations of the tax system in tandem (Benitez et al. 2023).

Without this broader institutional underpinning, additional revenue efforts risk being partial, inequitable, or unsustainable, undermining the fiscal resilience they are intended to build. Effective debt management requires not only controlling the overall level of debt but also managing its composition and risk profile, including maturity, currency, interest rate, refinancing, and creditor risks. Sound debt management acts as a key shock absorber during times of crisis. Poor borrowing choices made during periods of stress can worsen liquidity and solvency risks, particularly when governments turn to short-term solutions that are less transparent or less market based, such as private placements or collateralized borrowing. These instruments may provide immediate financing, but they can also increase rollover risks, reduce transparency, constrain future policy choices, and expose public assets or future revenues to claims. Governments should therefore design, implement, and communicate contingent borrowing plans before crises occur.

Conducting fiscal policy over the economic cycle. Economies that ran procyclical spending policies and persistent deficits over time faced economically larger and longer-lasting output losses from external shocks, whereas those that maintained countercyclical spending and ran primary surpluses, on average, experienced little to no losses. Dependence on commodities for exports and fiscal revenues makes commodity-exporting LMICs particularly exposed to swings in commodity prices. 68

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs During commodity price booms and the resulting rise in fiscal revenues, governments in those economies tend to increase spending. Without primary surpluses, those economies tend to have fewer fiscal resources to support activity and protect vulnerable populations when external shocks hit. Increased spending and debt accumulation during booms may also lead to a loss of market confidence during commodity price busts, requiring a large fiscal adjustment or contributing to debt distress (refer to box 2.3 for more details on external shocks and fiscal consolidation). The implication is clear: fiscal strategies that save windfalls during economic upturns, such as commodity booms, and deploy those savings during downturns allow governments to respond effectively when shocks arrive.

Box 2.3 External Shocks and Fiscal Consolidation Fiscal consolidation following a major external shock is particularly difficult and less likely to preserve growth. For example, consolidation episodes preceded by terms-of-trade shocks were significantly less successful in maintaining per capita growth rates near preconsolidation rates than episodes that were not preceded by such a shock (figure B2.3.1). This result reflects not only policy choices but also the persistent economic damage caused by the shock and the need for governments to support vulnerable households and economic activity before adjustment can begin.

Consolidation is often delayed even after fiscal balances become unsustainable, which carries compounding costs. Where the primary deficit was significantly larger than what would stabilize debt, countries tended to wait three to four years before embarking on meaningful fiscal consolidation (figure B2.3.2; Di Lorenzo and Lacey 2024). Political and social constraints are particularly binding in the aftermath of a shock, but delay can compound the eventual costs. Where large sustainability gaps (that is, the primary deficit was significantly larger than what would stabilize debt) persisted for four years or more, the median debt ratio increased by 17 percentage points of gross domestic product. Growth also weakened: during periods of sustained fiscal unsustainability, average real gross domestic product per capita growth fell to the 32nd percentile of each country’s own historical distribution. For countries facing high borrowing costs and limited market access, these findings underscore the value of early, credible, and growth-conscious corrective action. (Box continues on next page) 69

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs Establishing credible fiscal institutions and fiscal buffers. When a shock hits, the fiscal impact can be immediate and large, as spending needed to protect vulnerable communities rises while revenues fall. Governments can prepare for this tendency by establishing contingency reserves within the annual budget, natural disaster funds with clear rules governing their use and size calibrated to historical experience, and state-contingent debt instruments and other insurance mechanisms that transfer a portion of disaster risk to third parties (Polacek 2018). Well-designed fiscal rules can reinforce these buffers while allowing temporary, transparent flexibility during severe shocks. These instruments should be integrated into broader fiscal risk and debt-management frameworks. Contingent liabilities, including guarantees to state-owned enterprises, public-private partnerships, financial sector support, and disaster-related obligations, should be identified, monitored, and disclosed.

Medium-term expenditure frameworks offer one powerful mechanism for translating these commitments into practice, aligning spending with strategic priorities and ensuring the planning horizon needed to address future shocks before they arrive (World Bank 2012). Food Import Exposure, External Debt Burdens, and Healthy Diet Affordability Food imports are an important channel through which external shocks can affect food and nutrition security. They are particularly relevant as countries face an uncertain external environment, with geopolitical tensions, weather-related shocks, trade disruptions, and volatility in energy and fertilizer markets posing continued risks to global food markets and prices (FAO 2026; World Bank 2026a). Such shocks may be especially difficult to absorb in economies with high external debt burdens. In countries that rely more heavily on imported food, such shocks can translate into higher domestic food prices, with potentially important implications for household purchasing power, welfare, and diet quality, given the substantial share of food in household consumption, especially in lower-income countries (FAO and World Bank 2018).

Previous analysis in International Debt Report 2025 showed that higher external debt burdens were associated with higher levels of unaffordability of healthy diets across countries (World Bank 2025). This section extends that analysis by examining food import exposure as one important source of vulnerability to external shocks, including the importance of food in merchandise imports, reliance on imported supply across food groups, and the diversification of import sources. It also examines associations between external debt burdens and changes 71
INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 in healthy diet unaffordability over time, a broader outcome that reflects both food costs and people’s economic resources.

Food Import Shares in Poorer Economies Across the sample, which consists predominantly of LMICs, the share of food in merchandise imports generally declines as income per capita rises (figure 2.13, panel a). By contrast, economies with larger external debt burdens relative to exports also tend to have higher food import shares (figure 2.13, panel b).5 Both relationships matter for an economy’s capacity to manage food import exposure. Lower-income economies may have less room to absorb increases in import costs, and a high debt-to-exports ratio indicates that external debt is large relative to export earnings. During external shocks, higher import costs can therefore coincide with weaker economic and external buffers; export earnings may also decline, further increasing pressure on foreign exchange resources and raising the debt-to-exports ratio, even without an increase in the debt stock. Import Reliance and Debt Burdens Across Food Groups Aggregate food import shares do not show how strongly the domestic supply of individual food groups depends on international markets.

Net import reliance— net imports as a share of domestic supply quantity—varies substantially across the six food groups making up the Healthy Diet Basket (Bai, Herforth et al. 2025; Herforth et al. 2025). Among net importing economies, median reliance is highest for oils and fats, at 63.6 percent, followed by starchy staples, at 36.9 percent, and legumes, nuts, and seeds, at 34.1 percent. Median reliance is lower for animal-source foods, at 28.0 percent, and for vegetables and fruits, at 17.4 percent and 13.4 percent, respectively.

To identify economies where high reliance on food imports and elevated external debt burdens overlap, figure 2.13 applies two reference thresholds. For many economies, high import reliance coincides with elevated external debt burdens. Figure 2.14 highlights economies where external debt stocks are at least 150 percent of exports, as a reference point based on the threshold applied under the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative,6 and where net imports account for at least 30 percent of domestic supply in a given food group. The figure intends to identify the coexistence of these two sources of vulnerability, rather than to assess whether higher external debt is associated with greater reliance on food imports. This overlap is most common for oils and fats: 34 economies—about 42 percent of net importers in the group—meet both thresholds. The corresponding shares are about 28 percent for legumes, nuts, and seeds; 27 percent for starchy staples; 23 percent for animal-source foods; 16 percent for vegetables; and 15 percent for fruits. 72

2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs The overlap is widespread: 45 economies, of which 37 are MICs, meet both thresholds for at least one food group. Sixteen economies meet both thresholds in at least four food groups. Of those 16 economies, 10 are currently eligible for IDA financing: Bhutan, Cabo Verde, Comoros, Dominica, Fiji, The Gambia, São Tomé and Príncipe, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Suriname, and the Republic of Yemen. Eight of those 10 are also classified by the United Nations as either Small Island Developing States or landlocked developing countries. 73

text: 2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs Diversifying Import Sources to Improve Resilience Import reliance, however, captures only one dimension of exposure. Another is how concentrated imports are across source economies. An economy that sources a food group from a broader range of suppliers may have more options to adjust when trade with a particular exporter is disrupted than one that depends on only a few sources. Import source diversity is measured using the Shannon Diversity Index,7 which captures both the number of source economies and how evenly imports are distributed across them; higher values indicate greater diversification. Higher-income economies generally source food imports from a broader and more evenly distributed set of suppliers (Bai, Kaushik et al. 2025). text: 2. DEBT DyNAmIcs: POLIcy ImPLIcATIONs Among economies covered by this analysis, healthy diet unaffordability remains particularly high in LICs. The population-weighted prevalence of people unable to afford a healthy diet fell only marginally, from 77.4 percent in 2017 to 76.9 percent in 2025, and increased by 4.0 percentage points during 2019–21. Between 2017 and 2025, unaffordability declined from 58.5 to 45.2 percent in lower-middle-income economies and from 34.2 to 23.2 percent in upper-middle-income economies.

During 2017–19, the relationship between changes in healthy diet unaffordability and external debt burdens was weak and not statistically significant. The association became substantially stronger and statistically significant during 2019–21 and remained similarly strong and significant during 2021–23. In these periods, economies with higher debt stocks relative to export earnings tended to experience larger increases, or smaller declines, in healthy diet unaffordability. A doubling of the debt-to-exports ratio was associated with a more adverse change in unaffordability of approximately 1.6–1.8 percentage points. During 2023–25, the relationship weakened again and was no longer statistically significant. As revealed in this section, food import vulnerability reflects both reliance on imported supply and the concentration of import sources, and these dimensions can coincide with high external debt burdens. The period analysis adds an outcome perspective, showing that higher debt burdens are more strongly associated with nutrition security challenges during major external shocks, as reflected in changes in healthy diet unaffordability.

This pattern is consistent with the earlier framing of debt acting as an amplifier of vulnerability, and it highlights the importance of considering food import exposure and external debt together when assessing a country’s nutrition resilience to future external shocks. 3. Advancing Debt Transparency Introduction Over the past five years, the debt transparency agenda has moved decisively from an aspiration to a reality, translating commitments into tangible improvements in the coverage, accuracy, timeliness, and usability of debt data. This progress comes at a critical moment. As the prior chapters of this report show, the external debt stock of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and the costs of servicing that debt are at a record high, putting increasing pressure on public finances in many LMICs and crowding out critical social and development spending. In this environment, strengthening debt transparency is not merely a statistical objective; instead, it is an essential foundation for sound fiscal management, effective risk assessment, informed policy making, and financial stability. This chapter charts the progress made to date to enhance debt transparency in LMICs and discusses the important initiatives currently under way to scale up the debt transparency agenda.

Progress in Debt Transparency, 2020–25 Debt transparency is at the center of the World Bank Group’s engagement with its borrowers and partners. The policy commitment of the International Development Association (IDA) is to support debt sustainability and debt transparency through technical assistance, knowledge, and financing engagements. The Sustainable Development Finance Policy (SDFP), which became effective in July 2020, requires IDA-eligible borrowers at moderate or elevated risk of debt distress to take concrete policy performance actions (PPAs) to enhance debt transparency, strengthen debt management, and promote fiscal sustainability.1 These PPAs have been instrumental in incentivizing countries to embrace sustainable development financing, embed debt transparency reforms into national policy frameworks, and institutionalize transparent disclosure of public debt data.

The policy also leverages IDA’s global convening capacity to foster closer coordination among creditors to mitigate debt-related vulnerabilities, which has facilitated the reconciliation of data reported by borrowers to the World Bank Group Debtor Reporting System (DRS) with data made available by bilateral creditors. Consequently, asymmetries between the two data sets have 83

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 narrowed, further enhancing the coverage and accuracy of LMICs’ external debt data published by the World Bank Group in International Debt Statistics. Since the SDFP policy became effective, a total of 887 PPAs have been agreed, of which 60 percent focused on debt transparency and debt management and 40 percent on fiscal sustainability. In its first year in operation, fiscal year (FY) 2021, 55 IDA countries committed to 130 PPAs. By FY2026, these numbers had risen to 65 IDA countries implementing 159 PPAs, of which 55 percent focused on debt transparency and debt management. During the initial years of implementation, PPAs related to debt transparency focused on foundational measures aimed at disclosure of timely and comprehensive debt bulletins. More recently, the focus has shifted to monitoring and disclosure of contingent liabilities, borrowing by state-owned enterprises (SOEs), and actions that institutionalize timely debt monitoring and reporting. Overall, PPAs related to debt transparency have fallen from 32 percent of total PPAs in FY2021 to 10 percent in FY2026, reflecting progress made in disclosure of debt data.

However, the sustained implementation of reform measures in some IDA countries has proved challenging, particularly in states categorized as fragile and conflict affected. In addition, with tighter global financing conditions, some governments have turned to off-budget and increasingly complex debt instruments—including bilateral currency swaps, total return swaps, and collateralized loans—to meet financing needs, making it harder to assess public debt exposure.

The SDFP has consistently prioritized debt management, and the share of PPAs in debt management has remained steady, rising from 41 percent of total PPAs in FY2021 to 45 percent in FY2026. Debt management PPAs address risks stemming from high debt levels by ensuring compliance with nonconcessional borrowing ceilings. They also focus on strengthening institutional structures for debt management, including the creation of dedicated debt offices, strong legal and governance frameworks, and enhanced procedures for managing sovereign guarantees, on-lending, and borrowing by SOEs. Future PPAs in debt management will continue to address gaps in legislative frameworks, institutional fragmentation, and inadequate oversight of public borrowing. The SDFP also plays a catalytic role in advancing reforms related to the management of domestic debt and the development of domestic debt markets.

These reforms have included PPAs that supported the formulation and publication of medium-term debt strategies with clear targets for domestic and external borrowing in Fiji, the Kyrgyz Republic, Nigeria, the Solomon Islands, and Sri Lanka, and publication of annual borrowing plans that include domestic borrowing in the Central African Republic, Côte d’Ivoire, and St. Lucia. PPAs have also supported the development of operational guidelines for the issuance of government bonds in the domestic market in Bangladesh, the Solomon Islands, and Tonga; the strengthening of 84

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy investor relations in Togo; the publication of calendars for domestic bond issuance in Kosovo and Liberia; and measures to improve recording of domestic debt liabilities in Comoros. Going forward, the SDFP can play an even more critical role in advancing reforms to support domestic borrowing and development of investor relations and the implementation of a comprehensive legal and regulatory framework to govern domestic debt issuance, including clear delineation of the roles of the ministry of finance and the central bank. With IDA countries grappling with high debt burdens, rising financing needs, and a complex financing environment with options for riskier external financing arrangements, sound debt management of total public debt liabilities is more critical than ever.

The World Bank Group tracks progress in borrowing countries’ public debt dissemination practices on an annual basis. Its assessment of these outcomes is presented in a heat map that measures the strengths and weaknesses of the dissemination practices in 76 IDA-eligible countries across nine key indicators: data accessibility, instrument coverage, sectoral coverage, information on recently contracted external loans, periodicity, time lag, debt management strategy, annual borrowing plan, and additional statistics and memo items.2 The Debt Reporting Heat Map shows that, over the past five years, IDA-eligible borrowers have made significant progress in public debt disclosure practices. In 2020, only 36 IDA-eligible countries, 47 percent of the 76 countries covered by the heat map, published fully accessible public debt data. The 2025 heat map found that 54 countries, or 72 percent, had fully accessible public debt data, a 25-percentage-point gain from 2020 (figure 3.1).

Data accessibility in Sub-Saharan African countries has also improved significantly, rising from 19 countries (50 percent of countries in the region) that published fully accessible data in 2020, to 29 countries (or 76 percent) in 2025 despite a regression in accessibility of data in some countries. These countries include Ethiopia, where data accessibility had deteriorated since it defaulted on its international bond in 2023, and Senegal, following the revelation by the auditors of a large understatement in the official debt statistics. Even in countries that have accessible data, important information gaps persist. Instrument coverage has improved, with 45 countries assessed as having full coverage in 2025 compared to 33 countries in 2020, but progress has been slower than accessibility. Additionally, comprehensive sector coverage is limited, with subnational borrowing, contingent liabilities, and the obligations of SOE debt often excluded from the official public debt figure. Moreover, only about one-quarter of countries report instrument-level information on the terms of newly contracted debt. 85

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Improvements in data accessibility identified by the heat map are mirrored in enhanced timeliness and accuracy of reporting to the World Bank Group DRS. This is a mandatory reporting requirement for all countries that borrow from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) and IDA. Borrowers are increasingly meeting this requirement in accordance with the reporting timetable and are providing more comprehensive information on borrowing by central banks and SOEs. These advances have reduced gaps and asymmetries in global debt statistics, strengthened cross-country comparability, and solidified the DRS role as a cornerstone of global debt transparency.

For the end-2025 data reporting round, only 5.8 percent of the 121 LMICs obligated to report to the DRS missed the end-June 2026 deadline or failed to report, and most of those countries were at war or in conflict. This is a marked improvement over 2020, when 13 percent of countries were late reporters or nonreporters. Countries are also reporting earlier in the cycle, with 82 percent of countries submitting the end-2025 report by end-April—that is, only a four-month lag—which represents a 14-percentage-point increase from 2020 when 68 percent of countries reported by end-April (figure 3.2). 86

text: 3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy Significant progress has been made to improve the quality, coverage, and consistency of external debt statistics through systematic debtor-creditor reconciliation exercises. At the core of this initiative is the reconciliation of loan-by-loan information on public and publicly guaranteed external debt reported by borrowers to the DRS with corresponding data provided by bilateral creditors. This process enables cross-checking of data sets, identification of discrepancies, validation of loan terms and transactions, and filling of critical data gaps, all of which serve to enhance the accuracy of debt statistics.

Initiated in 2022, these exercises have become a central element of the broader debt transparency agenda, supporting more accurate debt monitoring, improved data validation, and better-informed debt analysis in IDA-eligible countries. The first reconciliation exercise, conducted using end-2021 data, covered 3,655 individual loans and loan tranches reported by 18 creditor countries, including all Group of Seven (G-7) members and 11 Paris Club creditors. Approximately 80 percent of loans were successfully matched, representing about 90 percent of total outstanding debt values, providing a first comprehensive assessment of discrepancies between debtor and creditor records. Despite a remaining overall difference of about 10 percent, the exercise provided critical insights into the nature and sources of discrepancies and established a strong foundation for future rounds. 87

text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 The third and most recent round of the reconciliation exercise, using end-2024 data, demonstrated substantial progress in aligning the debtor and creditor data sets for both scale and accuracy. Again, 18 creditors participated and together reported 4,875 individual loans and loan tranches, representing $63.4 billion in outstanding debt, out of which a total of 3,762 loans and loan tranches (77 percent) were matched to their counterpart in the DRS database (figure 3.3). For matched loans, creditor-reported claims of $58.0 billion differed by less than 1 percent from the comparable figure reported by debtors to the DRS, indicating that remaining gaps are relatively limited in magnitude.

The overall reporting gap, equivalent to $5.4 billion, masks much wider variations for individual creditors, but the reconciliation exercise found that gaps are also progressively narrowing. Figure 3.4 compares the total end-2024 claims reported by each of the 18 creditors with the total debt owed to each creditor that debtors reported to the DRS. Points on the dashed line indicate perfect alignment between debtor and creditor reporting. For 6 of the 18 participating creditors, the end-2024 claims align fully with the comparable figure reported by borrowers to the DRS, and for 2 creditors the gap was small. For other creditors, where larger differences were observed, these differences were typically concentrated in a small number of loans and found to be primarily the result of misclassification or differences in reporting norms, not true errors. As the chart also shows, discrepancies are not one directional: points above the dashed line indicate that claims reported by the creditor are higher than the comparable amount reported by the debtor, and points below the line reflect cases where the debtor figure is higher than the creditor.

The reconciliation exercises have highlighted that asymmetries between debtor and creditor data are not driven solely by gaps in debtor country reporting. Rather, they arise from several factors including differences in definitions, reporting practices, and institutional coordination. On the debtor side, these factors include (a) weak debt management, which limits timely, comprehensive recording of debt liabilities; (b) time lags in reporting new commitments and disbursements; (c) understatement of arrears, particularly penalty interest charges, often due to the complexity of how these are calculated; (d) failure to report, which results in estimated data by World Bank Group staff; and (e) misclassification of direct and guaranteed export credits.

Creditor-side factors include (a) lack of standard methodology and variation in national accounting norms; (b) the practice of some creditors to record disbursements as loan tranches without reference to the original loan commitment; (c) potential double-counting of bilateral lending delivered through common funds such as the European Economic Community–IDA trust fund and captured in the DRS as multilateral debt; and (d) inclusion of claims that are not external public sector, such as loans to private sector entities. 88
