text: INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Other reasons for asymmetries between the debtor and creditor data include recording of indemnification of payment arrears to private creditors on guaranteed export credits typically captured in debtor data only when a formal debt restructuring takes place. This problem is compounded by the fact that most creditors do not publish information on loans they have guaranteed. There is also an absence of a standard methodology applicable to both debtors and creditors for recording forgiveness of bilateral claims and bilateral debt swaps that extinguish external debt obligations in return for investment of the local currency equivalent in a dedicated fund for specific expenditures such as education or measures to mitigate climate change.

The reconciliation process has strengthened dialogue and underscored mutual accountability and the need for standardized reporting frameworks. Currently, DRS submissions provide more granular and complete information—such as loan-level details, disbursements, and terms—which are not always fully mirrored in creditor data sets. At the same time, the reconciliation exercises have played a critical role in identifying persistent data gaps, particularly regarding the liabilities of SOEs and structural weaknesses in debt reporting systems.

Since the reconciliation process began, tangible progress has taken place in creditor engagement. An increasing number of creditors provided a detailed response to follow-up queries and provided data clarification, contributing to more accurate gap-filling and reconciliation outcomes, reflecting a transition toward systematic collaboration. Building on this momentum will be critical to resolving remaining discrepancies and ensuring that the reconciliation exercise continues to deliver sustained improvements in data quality, transparency, and comparability. Overall, these data-sharing and reconciliation efforts have already significantly narrowed asymmetries between borrower and creditor data, strengthened the credibility of debt statistics, and improved the analytical foundation for monitoring debt vulnerabilities. As discussed in the following sections, continued collaboration, expanded participation, and ongoing methodological enhancements are expected to further advance data quality, transparency, and global comparability of debt statistics.

Scaling Up the Debt Transparency Agenda The DRS is a long-standing, cross-country comparable database on external debt for LMICs. Initially established in 1951 for institutional purposes to collect accurate and timely data on external public debt to evaluate borrowers’ 90

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy foreign currency obligations and assess creditworthiness, it evolved into a global public good, International Debt Statistics (IDS), which plays a central role in promoting debt transparency through the provision of standardized, cross-country comparable information on external debt levels in LMICs. Together, the DRS and the IDS are the backbone of the World Bank Group’s debt transparency architecture. Building a New Generation of Debt Statistics The DRS collects detailed, instrument-level information on public and publicly guaranteed external debt from IBRD and IDA borrowers to support the operational work of the World Bank Group. This work includes debt sustainability analysis, country diagnostics, debt transparency assessments, technical assistance, reform programs, and policy dialogue on macroeconomic outcomes and goals. Through its long-standing engagement with national debt offices, ministries of finance, and central banks, the DRS has become the central platform for methodological alignment, data validation, and institutional strengthening.

The IDS, the World Bank Group’s flagship statistical database on external debt, underpins the annual publication of the International Debt Report and serves as the primary global repository of external debt data for LMICs. It draws on data reported to the DRS and complementary information from other sources, including multilateral and bilateral creditors, international financial institutions, market data, and other statistical data sets to create the world’s most comprehensive and globally comparable statistical resource for policy makers, investors, researchers, and development partners. (Refer to annex 3A for more information on sources of debt statistics.) Complementary databases updated quarterly—Quarterly External Debt Statistics and Quarterly Public Sector Debt— provide high-frequency data that support the monitoring of evolving debt trends for the current year.

Modernizing and Expanding the DRS The DRS is currently undergoing the most extensive makeover since it was first implemented in the 1950s. The rationale for this modernization and expansion is threefold. The process aims to (a) introduce a new reporting framework and more comprehensive instrument-level reporting that responds to the changes in the global financial architecture and multiplicity of borrowing instruments now available to LMICs; (b) bring DRS reporting norms into conformity with the most recent international standards and definitions for recording and compiling debt statistics; and (c) take advantage of the latest advances in technology, including 91

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 where appropriate artificial intelligence, to streamline and simplify the reporting process, assist reporters with queries about reporting protocols, and validate the consistency of data. The new DRS framework, which will be finalized and rolled out in the coming year, represents a major step forward in strengthening the global debt data architecture.

The reporting framework is being expanded to introduce more comprehensive instrument-level reporting, including additional information on loan characteristics, debtor and creditor guarantees, collateral arrangements, debt reorganization, creditor attributes, and emerging financing instruments such as total return swaps, third party discounted buybacks, and asset-backed financing. The reporting requirements are designed to capture a comprehensive and much richer picture of all the basic characteristics of each debt instrument, such as borrower, lender, and associated terms. For example, additional reporting fields require the reporter to provide information on the type of debt security and the market and nominal value at the end of each reporting period. This information facilitates a more comprehensive analysis, such as an evaluation of the impact of market fluctuations on the valuation of debt instruments and alignment and comparison with the international statistical standards, in this case the liabilities recorded by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) International Investment Position.

The reporting standards and definitions are aligned to the latest international statistical standards, including the revised IMF directives on the compilation of balance of payments statistics from the seventh edition of the IMF’s Integrated Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (IMF 2025) and the United Nations Statistics Division’s 2025 System of National Accounts.

The new state-of-the-art DRS platform represents a radical change from the prior mechanism for the collection and compilation of debt data. It is structured around three key modules: data collection, data management, and reporting and analytics that take full advantage of the latest technological developments. The platform is designed to meet several key objectives: simplify and improve reporting efficiency for borrowers; incorporate automated data validation processes; enhance analytical capabilities; and facilitate greater interoperability with other international statistical systems. The development of the new DRS platform and its rollout are being coordinated with the Commonwealth Secretariat (Meridian) and the Debt Management and Financial Analysis System of UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), which provide the debt management software currently used by about 80 percent of DRS reporting countries. The goal is a seamless extraction, validation, and automated pass-through of data recorded by the borrowers in these systems to 92

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy the World Bank Group in a format that meets the DRS reporting requirement. The modernization of the DRS will also expand users’ access to IDS and allow them to generate customized aggregates and conduct deeper analytical work, while preserving the strict confidentiality of instrument-level information that borrowers share with the World Bank Group.

With the new reporting mechanism, DRS reporters will submit data through a web-based portal that streamlines and facilitates compliance with the World Bank Group reporting requirements. It provides reporters with an easy-to-use and efficient method for submitting both data and metadata securely. Reporting is structured around one reporting template that includes both public and publicly guaranteed and private nonguaranteed external debt and complementary modules, which replace the collective of DRS reporting forms previously used. The new portal enables DRS reporters to download the standardized reporting template and the related modules, and to upload data and validate them for consistency before submission to the World Bank Group. To facilitate reporting, it also includes a hyperlink to the DRS reporting manual and online how-to guidance for reporters when the reporting validating mechanism flags inconsistencies in the data being uploaded by the reporter.

Integrating Domestic Public Debt into the Debt Transparency Agenda A critical new frontier for the debt transparency agenda is the expansion of data coverage to domestic public debt, which has become an increasingly important share of LMICs’ public debt. In many of these countries, domestic public debt now accounts for 40–60 percent of total public debt, and in some of them it exceeds those shares. Despite the centrality of domestic debt levels to fiscal sustainability, sound monetary policy, and financial stability, data on domestic debt obligations remain fragmented, inconsistently defined, and only partially captured in international data sets. In marked contrast to external public debt, no comprehensive global platform currently exists to systematically collect and disseminate detailed, comprehensive, and cross-country comparable domestic public debt data for LMICs.

The World Bank Group initiative to extend the DRS to domestic public debt represents a unique contribution to the global data architecture. It is the only framework currently in development that aims to bring together detailed, standardized, and cross-country comparable domestic public debt statistics for LMICs. The integration of domestic and external debt into a single, coherent reporting system to the DRS opens the door, for the first time, to the creation of a comprehensive and unified picture of public sector liabilities. This picture will provide the wherewithal to make a far more accurate assessment of a 93
INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 country’s debt sustainability and an evaluation of the fiscal risks domestic debt obligations pose.

This initiative presents institutional and technical challenges. Extensive diagnostic work, including surveys and pilot exercises conducted by the World Bank Group with DRS reporting countries and partner institutions that support them— including the IMF, the Commonwealth Secretariat, and UNCTAD—identified a vast and complex array of instruments for raising financing in domestic markets. In many LMICs, domestic debt is managed by multiple entities, including ministries of finance, central banks, and subnational governments, and recorded in different systems using a variety of classifications. An important element of the new reporting framework will be the introduction of a standardized reporting template based on international definitions and classifications. It will be complemented by a detailed reporting manual and comprehensive guidelines on consolidation of domestic and external public debt across different levels of government to derive comprehensive and accurate measures of total public sector liabilities.

To support implementation, the World Bank Group is developing methodological guidance on compiling and reporting domestic debt statistics in collaboration with the IMF, the Commonwealth Secretariat, UNCTAD, and other international partners.

Implementation of the domestic debt module represents a major expansion of the DRS and will require significant institutional reforms and technical enhancements in many LMICs. These changes include strengthening legal mandates for data collection, improving coordination across public sector entities, and upgrading debt management systems. In view of these needs, the domestic debt reporting framework will be introduced on a phased and voluntary basis, beginning with central government debt and progressively expanding to full public sector coverage, thereby allowing LMICs to participate according to their capacity while simultaneously benefiting from targeted technical assistance. The World Bank Group is confident that, over time, full integration of domestic and external debt data into a unified reporting framework can be achieved with a game-changing impact on debt transparency. Comprehensive debt statistics will provide critical insights into total public debt burdens, maturity concentration, interest rate exposure, and rollover risks, and will enhance the reconciliation of debt records with fiscal and monetary statistics and overall macroeconomic surveillance.

Institutionalizing Debtor-Creditor Data Sharing and Reconciliation The debtor-creditor reconciliation exercise has become an annual program supported by continuous and structured engagement with participating 94

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy G-7 and Paris Club creditors. As already illustrated, these reconciliation exercises have been instrumental in improving data-sharing practices, enhancing methodological alignment, and expanding the scope and coverage of the exercise. The reconciliation of data reported by debtors to the DRS with the comparable creditor records has played a critical role in identifying structural data gaps and has demonstrated how detailed loan-level data sharing and dialogue can lead to tangible results, including the resolution of large discrepancies and the closing of previously unreported debt positions. These results have also reinforced the need for continuous dialogue and data reconciliation, and adoption of standardized reporting norms to sustain concordance between debtor and creditor data.

Efforts are already under way to broaden participation beyond the current group of G-7 and Paris Club bilateral creditors. Ongoing discussions with key Group of Twenty creditors are positive, and the expectation is that additional bilateral creditors will participate in the next end-2025 data reconciliation exercise. In this context, an important development is the publication in July 2026 by the World Bank Group Chief Statistician of the “Protocol on the Handling of Creditor Data Submitted to the World Bank Debtor Reporting System” (Chief Statistician 2026). It sets out the terms on which these data are shared and the confidentiality rules that apply to them, providing reassurance for creditors that the data will be used strictly for purposes of data reconciliation. This has been an important factor in the creditors’ decision to share the very detailed information required for the reconciliation exercise. Over time, the plan is to extend participation to all official creditors, both bilateral and multilateral, and to encourage private creditors to participate.

The World Bank Group is actively engaged in devising mechanisms to streamline and automate the reconciliation process (refer to box 3.1 on the Indonesia Loan Clearing Module Pilot Project). There is also a proposal to integrate a creditor reporting module into the DRS cloud-based platform to enable creditors to submit data electronically and securely. This capability would replace the current email-based submission process and significantly improve the efficiency, standardization, and security of creditor reporting. In parallel, the creditor reporting template is being redefined to capture more granular information, particularly on loan terms, transactions, guarantees, and restructuring details. These details are already made available to the DRS by debtors, and the objective is to enhance comparability across the data sets and eliminate all discrepancies. 95

Box 3.1 The Indonesia Loan Clearing Module Pilot Project New standards and protocols for debt data reconciliation supported by innovative information technology solutions to systematically digitalize and automatically reconcile public loan data have the potential to ensure better quality recording and save time and effort. The World Bank Group is already evaluating such standards and protocols. In 2025, it launched a pilot project in Indonesia, funded by the Japanese Ministry of Finance, to develop a Loan Clearing Module to facilitate information sharing between borrowers and official creditors. This module acts as a platform for information sharing between creditors’ data systems and those of local debt management offices. For each new transaction (that is, new loan signed, payment, disbursement, or modification), the originator would create a new data file electronically transmitted to the platform according to standardized templates. The counterpart then validates the information and automatically transfers the data as needed into its own debt recording system.

In its first phase, this project seeks to reconcile loans issued by Indonesia’s largest external lenders (the Japan International Cooperation Agency, the Asian Development Bank, and the World Bank Group), before including a wider group of Indonesian official and potential private sector creditors in the second phase. Implementation of the pilot project in Indonesia has already demonstrated the technical feasibility of continuous synchronization and validation of debtor and creditor data. The debt office has already automatically transferred World Bank Group loan data and uploaded them into the local debt system; as of May 2026, the platform had successfully exchanged and validated a total of 761 loan records, and 642 subefforts are under way to cover other official creditors. Once fully operational, the Loan Clearing Module codes could be made available to other countries, potentially serving as an international platform for debt data reconciliation, providing a new, real-time source of fully validated debt statistics.

Capacity Building for Stronger Debt Statistics and Transparency Debt transparency involves much more than encouraging debtors and their creditors to disclose additional data. Advancing the debt transparency agenda ultimately depends on strengthening loan records, disbursement records, and payment records. Producing accurate and comprehensive data to the standard required for informed fiscal and debt management decision-making requires strong institutional arrangements, rigorous legal and governance structures, consistent statistical standards, and robust validation processes. Building the Foundations of Debt Transparency Capacity building is an integral part of the World Bank Group’s debt transparency agenda. Over the past five years, the Debt Statistics Team has 96

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy contributed to 23 courses and workshops at the global, regional, and country levels. These opportunities were complemented by targeted technical assistance for individual IDA-eligible countries and continuous engagement with other international organizations and regional banks providing comparable capacity-building services. Support from the Debt Statistics Team is broad-based and includes presentations on best practice in monitoring and recording debt data, advice on how to manage the public debt portfolio and contingent liabilities, and guidance for understanding and adopting international statistical standards and definitions. This support is combined with assistance on how to strengthen institutional systems and human resources responsible for compilation and dissemination of debt statistics at the national level and to international data sets. It also builds awareness on how these data factor into decision-making regarding public borrowing and debt sustainability within the broader framework of macroeconomic policies.

The delivery mechanism has also evolved with a heightened emphasis on practical training aimed at strengthening the entire debt data production chain. This training includes all aspects of the data collection process, from recording individual debt instruments, to institutional coordination to monitor stocks and flows, data validation and reconciliation, and dissemination and use of comprehensive debt statistics for analyses and use by policy makers.

The modernization and expansion of the DRS serves as an important anchor for structuring the capacity-building program in debt data management. It currently covers about 120 World Bank Group borrowing countries and more than 50,000 active loan records, with approximately 2,500–3,000 new loans reported each year. Maintaining a system of this scale and ensuring the integrity of the data require sustained investment in national reporting capacity. Practical training sessions are not limited to familiarizing debt managers with the new and very different DRS reporting structure. They include equally, if not more, important training in how to implement international statistical standards to categorize and compile debt data. In this context, the overarching goal is to also transmit the skills required to determine if data are complete, internally consistent, appropriately classified, and aligned with international statistical standards. Workshops provide hands-on experience and test runs of the revised classifications and reporting requirements, and explain the links between DRS concepts and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014).

Such alignments are important because countries should not have to maintain parallel conceptual frameworks for national external debt statistics and international reporting. Moreover, consistency between the two reduces the reporting burden, improves comparability, and enhances the use of DRS data for the countries’ own debt management and analytical purposes. 97

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 The agenda is also expanding beyond external debt. The voluntary rollout of reporting on domestic public debt creates an opportunity to strengthen countries’ capacity to produce a more comprehensive picture of total public sector indebtedness. Over time, this capacity can help reduce the historical divide between external and domestic debt reporting, and support more integrated analysis of countries’ overall debt vulnerabilities.

A Partnership-Based Model to Develop Capacity The World Bank Group’s approach to capacity building to strengthen debt management is multifaceted and includes regional courses, country-specific technical assistance, and peer learning delivered in partnerships with other international organizations. Regional workshops are typically organized as intensive five-day programs combining technical presentations with exercises, country cases, simulations, and structured discussions. They allow participants to apply statistical concepts to the practical problems they encounter in their daily work. Participation extends beyond debt management offices, and the World Bank Group strives to bring together, whenever possible, staff from central banks, ministries of finance, statistical agencies, and other institutions involved in producing debt information. This cross-institutional approach is important because weaknesses in debt statistics often arise not from a lack of information but from fragmentation of that information across multiple government institutions.

Bringing these institutions together can improve understanding of responsibilities, facilitate data sharing, and strengthen consistency across national data sets. Partnerships with institutions like the IMF, the Commonwealth Secretariat, and UNCTAD strengthen the multifaceted approach by contributing to regional training programs, connecting statistical standards to debt management practices and reporting requirements, and underscoring the imperatives of ensuring debt data management systems are updated and validated on a daily basis. Cooperation with the Commonwealth Secretariat and UNCTAD is particularly valuable now, as the redesigned DRS is being incorporated into the debt management systems they have created and maintain in order to embed methodological changes into national operating environments and to automate DRS reporting requirements.

Responding to an Increasingly Complex Debt Landscape Capacity building has also expanded to address areas where weaknesses in coverage can have significant implications for assessments of public debt and fiscal risks. One such area is nonguaranteed borrowing by SOEs and other public sector entities. Identifying these liabilities can be difficult when information is dispersed across institutions or when debt management systems focus primarily on central government borrowing. Training therefore helps participants identify 98

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy institutional coverage gaps and understand how nonguaranteed and contingent liabilities should be captured and classified. More attention is also being given to emerging and complex instruments. As sovereign financing evolves and lending instruments become more complex, methodological guidance on how to account for them and expertise in assessing the risks they may pose takes on added importance.

An important evolution in the capacity-building program has been its integration into the World Bank Group’s mainstream work on data quality and debt sustainability. Data discrepancies are increasingly being seen not simply as errors to be corrected but as diagnostic information that offers insights into weaknesses in national systems. The annual reconciliation of debtor and creditor information is a good example. Differences may reveal problems in creditor classification, exchange rate conversion, recording of arrears, treatment of restructurings, institutional coverage, or the timing of transactions. Working through these discrepancies directly with country authorities provides an opportunity to identify their causes and improve compilation practices at the source. The same principle underpins the work of harmonizing the data to the DRS and the data national authorities provide for the debt sustainability analyses conducted jointly by the IMF and the World Bank Group. Improvements in the timeliness and quality of reporting to the DRS by IDA-eligible countries offer clear indications that these measures are having a positive knock-on effect.

Providing Continuous and Scalable Learning Traditional face-to-face training is valuable and essential, particularly where participants need to work through country-specific institutional and methodological issues. But the scale of training required, coupled with the turnover of staff in national debt offices, is such that capacity building cannot be delivered exclusively through periodic workshops. The next phase is therefore moving toward a more continuous model combining regional training, targeted technical assistance, methodological guidance, and digital learning. Training materials are being developed in conjunction with the updated DRS Manual and reporting guidance, and collaboration with the World Bank Group Data Academy can provide structured e-learning modules that countries can access between formal training events.

This approach can create a more sustainable capacity-building ecosystem with introductory modules providing a common foundation for new debt compilers and specialized modules to address topics such as restructuring, arrears, contingent liabilities, creditor classification, domestic debt, and new financial instruments. Online tools such as validation guides and step-by-step guides to reporting templates, test exercises, and case studies can support participants 99

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 after formal training has ended. This support will enable regional or country workshops to focus on practical applications and more complex cases and create the space for peer learning, which will remain an important part of this model. Countries frequently face similar challenges, and regional workshops provide an opportunity to exchange practical solutions and institutional experiences that cannot easily be captured in manuals. Group exercises and simulations have demonstrated the value of allowing participants to work jointly through real reporting and classification problems.

From Capacity Building to Sustainable Debt Transparency Success is not measured by the number of people trained but by the improvement in the coverage, quality, and transparency of the debt data countries produce. It requires institutional and instrument coverage, more timely submissions, fewer unexplained discrepancies, better reconciliation between national and international data sets, and greater public availability of debt information, and can be achieved only by tailoring and adapting capacity-building activities to country circumstances and needs. For some countries, the primary need is methodological training; for others, it centers on institutional improvements in debt management systems, assistance in reconciling databases, or extending coverage of public sector debt to SOEs, contingent liabilities, or domestic debt. Diagnostic information from DRS reporting, data validation, debtor-creditor reconciliation, and comparisons with other international data sets are increasingly being used to target technical assistance to areas where they will have the greatest impact.

The World Bank Group’s role extends beyond collecting debt data, to supporting LMICs to build the human capital and institutional arrangements and the systems required to produce them. Sustainable improvements in debt transparency depend on strong national institutions with the capacity to generate reliable information.

As both external and domestic financing for LMICs becomes more complex, this investment will become even more important. New creditors, new instruments, growing domestic debt markets, and greater attention to public sector and contingent liabilities are expanding the information countries need to manage them. Capacity building must evolve alongside these developments if borrowers are to keep pace. Ultimately, more reliable debt data and stronger national capacity go hand in hand and reinforce each other. More robust institutions produce better statistics, which in turn underscore inherent weaknesses and permit technical support to be targeted more effectively; and stronger national systems make improvements in debt transparency more durable. Capacity building is not complementary to the debt transparency agenda; rather, it is one of the foundations on which the agenda stands. 100

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy Debt Asymmetries Transparent external and public debt data are fundamental to assessing LMICs’ financial situations. These data provide the foundation for debt sustainability analysis, managing fiscal and monetary policy, and disclosure of the level and composition of existing obligations to creditors, investors, development partners, and citizens. The expectation is that debt transparency will bring clarity with a definitive account of a country’s debt situation. All too often, however, the debt data disseminated by LMICs differ from creditors’ claims, raising doubts about data accuracy, under-recording, or, worse, deliberate nondisclosure and hidden debt. Although these situations are sometimes the case, the primary challenge to the accuracy, credibility, and comparability of debt data is asymmetries, particularly between debtor- and creditor-reported figures.

Addressing Debt Asymmetries Is Key to Debt Transparency Asymmetries in debt data arise primarily from inconsistent methodological definitions and accounting practices in debtor and creditor countries and other institutions that compile and disseminate debt data. These divergent practices present a minefield for users trying to compare debtor and creditor data or to make cross-country comparisons across groups of debtors or creditors. In extreme cases discrepancies as large as 30 percent of gross domestic product have been observed in debt stock figures purporting to have the same coverage. Issues as simple as classification of domestic and external debt on a currency basis will likely result in a very different number for external debt stocks than the one disseminated by the World Bank Group in IDS, which uses the international standard residency criterion. Conversely, IDS may legitimately record a lower figure for external debt owed to a creditor than the creditor itself records. This discrepancy occurs because the IDS figure excludes loans to nonguaranteed private sector borrowers, not separately identifiable in the aggregate data reported to the DRS.

Mitigating data asymmetries is key to being able to validate debt data and confirm those data to be comprehensive and accurate, a core objective of the debt transparency agenda. The Reasons for Asymmetries in Debt Data One of the key reasons for debt data asymmetries is the existence of multiple data sources. The primary sources are debtor and creditor accounting, and data collection frameworks. The main actors in debtor countries are debt management offices, finance ministries, central banks, and national statistical agencies, which have varying institutional mandates and data collection mechanisms. In creditor countries, there are the databases of bilateral lending agencies 101

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 such as aid ministries, official export credit agencies, and public sector banks. International financial institutions like the IMF and the World Bank Group are important creditors, and they play a central role in the compilation of global debt and other external sector statistics. Similarly, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) collects and disseminates data on aid flows and bilateral loans, and the Bank for International Settlements does the same for financing by the banking sector. There are also databases that capture information on market-based sources of financing collated by private companies such as Dealogic. Annex 3A provides a summary of the focus and coverage of the key debt databases.

Asymmetries in debt data also stem from a whole range of factors, including differences in coverage, timing of recording, institutional practice, and delayed reporting by borrowers and creditors. Coverage often differs—debtor-based systems may exclude private nonguaranteed borrowing, whereas creditor-side data likely capture these flows more comprehensively. Recording practices vary: some compilers adopt accrual-based accounting (recognizing transactions when obligations arise), whereas others use the cash basis method (recording payments when they are made). These divergent practices lead to timing and value mismatches. Another common source of asymmetry is valuation, which uses different exchange rates or accounting methods. For example, compilations based on the face value versus the market value for bond issues will result in very different figures for outstanding balances. Divergent valuation rules for inflation-indexed or floating-rate instruments can further widen the gap between data sets.

Numerous inconsistencies also occur in instrument classification and sectorization—that is, how borrowers are classified and captured in public or private sector debt data. Methodological discrepancies are frequently embedded in national statistical practices and international reporting frameworks, creating challenges for users trying to reconcile external and public debt data across sources. Trade credits and advances may be included in external debt statistics in some countries and unaccounted for in others. Loans extended by state-owned banks may be classified as public debt on the creditor side but recorded as private debt by the debtor. Differences in the classification of borrowers, particularly SOEs, central banks, and government-guaranteed entities, can lead to significant discrepancies between data sets. Some statistical systems treat SOEs as part of the public sector, whereas others classify them as private unless explicitly guaranteed. Similarly, contingent liabilities and guarantees may be included in debt totals in some frameworks but excluded until they are triggered in others, producing further divergence in reported figures. 102

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy International institutions have stepped up efforts to harmonize the compilation of debt statistics. The IMF and the Task Force on Finance Statistics promote the use of standardized statistical frameworks such as External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014) and are currently supporting updates to better account for evolving borrowing trends, including state-contingent debt instruments and collateralized borrowing. The Quarterly External Debt Statistics platform, comanaged by the IMF and the World Bank Group, enables countries to submit quarterly data aligned with international standards, thereby improving consistency and transparency. Other important initiatives include the World Bank Group Debt Transparency Initiatives and the IDA Sustainable Development Finance Policy, both of which tie financial support to improvements in debt reporting.

As already discussed, the core objective of the major revamp of the World Bank Group DRS is harmonization of reporting standards and definitions for LMICs with agreed international methodology, including the IMF’s Integrated Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (IMF 2025) and the United Nations Statistics Division’s 2025 System of National Accounts, supported by dedicated capacity building. Many asymmetries could also be avoided through automation and system integration. Developing centralized platforms that link balance of payments, international investment position statistics, and external debt data, and enable interoperability between debt management systems and other external sector statistics databases, would force consistency and minimize manual errors. Emerging technologies such as discrepancy detectors powered by artificial intelligence or SDMX-based data exchanges would further modernize data compilation workflows.

From Granular Data to Actionable Knowledge For more than seven decades, the World Bank Group DRS has transformed detailed information reported by borrowing countries into one of the world’s most comprehensive sources of internationally comparable external debt statistics. It provides a statistical infrastructure for understanding not simply how much countries owe but who borrowed from whom, through which instruments, and on what terms, and how those obligations evolve over time. At its core, the program is a continuous data-to-knowledge process. Detailed information reported by borrowing countries is systematically validated, reconciled, and standardized before being transformed into internationally comparable debt statistics. These statistics are then analyzed and placed in their broader economic and financial context, turning granular country reporting 103

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 into evidence that can inform debt management, debt sustainability assessments, financing decisions, and the global policy debate. The World Bank Group debt transparency work is built as a continuous chain of value through three-tier architecture (refer to annex 3B for more information on the World Bank Group Debt Statistics three-tier architecture): DRS provides the granular evidence, IDS transforms that evidence into trusted and transparent statistical facts, and the International Debt Report (IDR) converts those facts into analysis and actionable knowledge. Together, these three tiers connect country-level debt reporting to the broader development and policy agenda. A loan reported by a national debt office can serve as a globally comparable indicator, reveal a change in creditor or financing patterns, expose an information gap or emerging vulnerability, inform a debt sustainability assessment or restructuring discussion, and contribute to international policy discussions on sustainable finance and debt transparency.

This process also works in reverse. Transparency gaps, new financing instruments, emerging vulnerabilities, and methodological challenges identified through IDS and IDR analysis feed directly back into the DRS. They inform improvements in reporting requirements, classifications, validation rules, reconciliation procedures, methodological guidance, and engagement with both borrowers and creditors. Debt transparency is therefore not a one-time disclosure exercise but a continuous cycle of reporting, validation, reconciliation, dissemination, analysis, and improvement. This architecture is also central to the World Bank Group’s broader debt transparency agenda. Greater transparency about the amount, composition, terms, and creditors of public debt is essential for sound debt management, credible debt sustainability assessments, effective restructuring, and informed lending and investment decisions. By strengthening reporting standards, improving data quality, reconciling debtor and creditor records, expanding the information available to users, and identifying remaining data gaps, the DRS provides the statistical foundation on which greater debt transparency can be built.

This approach also reflects an important evolution in the international debt transparency agenda: responsibility does not rest solely with borrowing countries. Comprehensive debt transparency requires coordinated action by borrowers, bilateral and multilateral creditors, private lenders, international financial institutions, and other stakeholders. The World Bank Group’s role is increasingly to connect these actors around common definitions, stronger reporting practices, better reconciliation, and more accessible and reliable debt information. 104

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy The result is more than a debt database. It is a global statistical infrastructure for debt transparency that connects individual debt obligations to a broader understanding of financing flows, creditor relationships, fiscal pressures, and debt sustainability, while helping make sovereign borrowing increasingly visible, comparable, credible, and accountable.

Ultimately, strengthening debt transparency comes down to ensuring that public borrowing remains a tool for development rather than a source of vulnerability. By improving the availability and reliability of debt data, countries are better equipped to manage risks, design effective policies, and engage transparently with stakeholders. For creditors and markets, enhanced transparency supports more accurate risk assessment and more efficient allocation of capital. For the international community, it contributes to a more stable and resilient global financial system. Sustained investment in this agenda is not only advisable, but it is also necessary for positive long-term development outcomes. Annex 3A. Sources of Debt Statistics Debt statistics originate from a diverse set of sources, classified broadly into debtor-based and creditor-based data sets. Each has unique strengths as well as limitations that may lead to discrepancies.

Debtor-Based Sources Debtor-based data are sourced from countries that borrow, typically through institutions such as finance ministries, debt management offices, or central banks. These data are reported to international sources like the World Bank Group’s DRS and the IMF’s Balance of Payments and International Investment Position. Although rich in detail, debtor-based data sources reflect the borrower’s operational realities and often omit or underreport certain types of debt, such as short-term borrowing and borrowing in the form of debt securities and private sector liabilities, or debt from SOEs without sovereign guarantees. The DRS covers long-term public and publicly guaranteed external debt, along with aggregate information for private nonguaranteed debt when available. Data are reported on an instrument-by-instrument basis, providing detailed information on terms, disbursements, debt service, and outstanding amounts. The key strength of the DRS is the depth and consistency of coverage for LMICs, enabling granular analysis.

Its main limitation is the absence of short-term debt and certain debt instruments, such as pension fund liabilities (owed to national households but held by nonresidents), currency and deposits, and trade credit and advances. Moreover, the aggregation of private nonguaranteed debt reporting 105
INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 may mask incomplete coverage and can obscure the characteristics of specific instruments.

The IMF’s Balance of Payments and International Investment Position frameworks capture external debt as part of the broader international accounts, including components such as direct investment debt, portfolio debt, and other investment debt (for example, loans and trade credit and advances). The key strength of these data is their alignment with global macroeconomic accounts, ensuring comparability across countries. The principal limitation is that they are published in aggregate form, masking important details such as the instrument type, currency composition, interest rate structure, maturity profile, creditor sector, and other specifics like collateralization, governing law, and repayment schedules. It warrants mention that the use of original maturity in the International Investment Position, and thus the unavailability of statistics on a remaining maturity basis, significantly limits the use of International Investment Position external debt–related statistics for debt sustainability analysis.

National debt management systems such as the Commonwealth Secretariat’s Meridian, UNCTAD’s Debt Management and Financial Analysis System, and country-specific custom-built platforms are used by borrowers to record, monitor, and manage public debt, often serving as the source of data submitted to the World Bank Group or IMF. Their strength lies in the operational detail they capture to support day-to-day debt management decisions. Their limitation lies in inconsistency in how these systems are used and the accuracy and completeness of the data recorded in them. These strengths and limitations vary significantly and largely mirror a country’s institutional and technical capacity. Creditor-Based Sources The creditor-based sources reflect the viewpoint of the lending institutions, such as donor governments, commercial banks, and bondholders. These sources include the OECD’s Creditor Reporting System, the Bank for International Settlements statistics, and data collated by the Paris Club. Although these sources often provide visibility into bilateral and private sector lending, their coverage may be limited geographically or in terms of the types of instruments covered.

Discrepancies between these sources are at the heart of many data asymmetries. These sources reflect the view of those who provide financing, often more complete for bilateral and private sector debt. The OECD Creditor Reporting System tracks official bilateral loans and grants from members of the Development Assistance Committee and from export credit agencies. It contains detailed information on aspects such as concessionality, maturity, and the intended purpose of financing. Its key strength is its dedicated 106

3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy focus on development finance, providing detailed insights into aid flows and related terms. Its main limitation is its restricted coverage to official and officially supported lending by OECD member countries.

The Bank for International Settlements compiles data from commercial banks on cross-border claims and liabilities through two primary data sets: Locational Banking Statistics, which reports according to the location of the reporting bank; and Consolidated Banking Statistics, which reports banks’ global claims on other countries. Its strength lies in providing timely data on private financial flows, particularly from the banking sector, making it valuable for near-real-time monitoring of cross-border lending trends. Its limitation is that the data are not at the loan level and may not align with debtor country classifications, reducing its utility for detailed debt instrument analysis or reconciliation with national statistics. The Paris Club, private sector data collection entities like Dealogic, and some export credit agencies supply information on bilateral debt restructurings, syndicated loans and international bond issues, and direct and guaranteed export credits. Their strength is that they offer unique insights into certain types of financing—such as officially supported export credits and market-based lending— that are often underrepresented in other data sets.

Their limitation is that the information is fragmented, not systematically compiled, and often not publicly available in a timely manner, creating gaps in comprehensive debt monitoring. Annex 3B. The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Three-Tier Architecture The World Bank Group Debt Statistics Program operates through a three-tier architecture that progressively transforms granular country reporting into internationally comparable statistics and policy-relevant knowledge, while strengthening transparency at every stage of the process (figure 3B.1). Tier 1: DRS—The Granular Data Foundation Established in 1951, the DRS is one of the world’s longest-running sovereign debt reporting systems. Today, it covers roughly 120 low- and middle-income reporting economies and provides a uniquely detailed historical record extending over more than 70 years. IBRD and IDA borrowers report detailed information on their long-term public and publicly guaranteed external debt, including new commitments, outstanding stocks, and annual transactions. Private nonguaranteed external debt is also incorporated in aggregate form.
At this first tier, the data answer four fundamental questions: Who borrowed? From whom? On what terms? And what happened to the debt over time? These questions are 107

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 central to debt transparency, particularly as sovereign financing becomes more complex. LMICs increasingly combine traditional bilateral and multilateral loans with syndicated lending, international bonds, collateralized financing, debt swaps, buybacks, and more sophisticated restructuring operations. The DRS provides the granular data infrastructure needed to identify, measure, and track debt exposures over time. At the individual debt level, it captures detailed information on borrowers, creditors, instruments, currencies, commitments, disbursements, debt service, arrears, and restructurings, providing insight not only into the amount of debt outstanding but also into its composition, financing terms, repayment profile, and evolution. As sovereign financing instruments and practices continue to evolve, DRS reporting requirements, classifications, and methodological guidance are continuously strengthened to ensure that this growing complexity is reflected in comprehensive, consistent, and increasingly complete coverage of countries’ debt obligations and financing arrangements.

Tier 2: IDS—From Granular Records to Trusted and Transparent Statistics Debt transparency depends not only on the availability of information but also on its quality, consistency, comparability, and credibility. Individual debt records become meaningful global statistics only after they have been standardized and made comparable across countries and over time. This transformation takes place through the production of the IDS database. The second tier moves beyond 108

text: 3. ADvANcINg DEBT TRANsPARENcy individual transactions to answer the following questions: What happened? Where did it happen? How are financing patterns changing? How do countries compare? And where do important information gaps remain? The statistical production process involves the compilation of the external debt statistics using standardized methodologies, definitions, and classifications. This process is critical to ensure that published statistics accurately reflect countries’ debt. IDS adds value across four critical dimensions: (a) comparability, through common concepts and classifications across economies; (b) consistency, through reconciliation of stocks, flows, transactions, and revisions; (c) historical series, which make it possible to identify structural changes in global financing; and (d) accessibility, through public databases, downloadable data sets, country and regional tables, and analytical products. Tier 3: IDR—From Trusted Statistics to Actionable Knowledge The annual IDR represents the analytical tier of architecture. It combines the depth of the underlying DRS information and the consistency of IDS statistics with economic and policy analysis.

Where the DRS captures what countries report, and IDS establishes what happened, the IDR examines why it happened, why it matters, who is most exposed and more vulnerable, and what policy makers should watch next. For more than five decades, the World Bank Group’s annual debt publication has documented major transformations in international development finance, from the debt crises of the 1980s and the emergence of global bond markets, to debt-relief initiatives, the rise of new bilateral and private creditors, increasingly complex financing instruments, and today’s environment of elevated borrowing costs and debt service pressures. The IDR places these developments in their wider economic context. It serves as both an analytical publication and an important instrument of the World Bank Group’s debt transparency agenda by highlighting where improvements in reporting, disclosure, creditor information, and debt management practices are most needed.

Data Sources The principal source of information for the tables in International Debt Report 2026 is the International Debt Statistics database, which is based on reports to the World Bank through the World Bank’s Debtor Reporting System (DRS) from member countries that have received either International Bank for Reconstruction and Development loans or International Development Association credits. The DRS has its origin in the World Bank’s need to monitor and assess the financial position of its borrowers. Since 1951, borrowers have been required to provide statistics on their public external debt and private sector debt that benefit from a public guarantee. Reporting countries submit reports on the annual status, transactions, and terms of the long-term external debt of public agencies and that of private ones guaranteed by a public agency in the debtor country. The DRS maintains these records on a loan-by-loan basis. In 1973, coverage of the DRS was expanded to include private sector nonguaranteed borrowing; however, for this category of debt, data are provided by borrowers in aggregate rather than loan by loan.

Data submitted to the DRS are processed in the World Bank External Debt system, along with additional information received from the African Development Bank, the Asian Development Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the Inter-American Development Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and institutions of the World Bank Group (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and International Development Association). The World Bank External Debt is an internal system of the World Bank. Among its outputs is the International Debt Statistics database, from which the tables and data visualizations in this publication and the online database are produced. Data on exports and imports (on a balance of payments basis), international reserves, current account balances, foreign direct investment on equity, portfolio equity flows, and primary income on foreign direct investment are drawn mainly from the International Monetary Fund, supplemented by UN Trade and Development reports and country data. Balance of payments data are presented according to the sixth edition of the International Monetary Fund’s Balance of Payments Manual.

Official aid flows come from data collected and published by the Development Assistance Committee of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Short-term external debt data are as reported by debtor countries or are estimates based on the Bank for International Settlements 243

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 quarterly series of commercial banks’ claims on low- and middle-income countries. For some countries, estimates were prepared by pooling creditor and debtor information. Data on the gross national income of most low- and middle-income countries are collected from national statistical organizations or central banks by visiting and resident World Bank missions.

Every effort has been made to ensure the accuracy and completeness of the external debt statistics. Coverage has been improved through the efforts of the reporting agencies and close collaboration between the World Bank and its partners, the Commonwealth Secretariat and UN Trade and Development, which provide debt recording and reporting systems across the globe, as well as through the work of the World Bank missions, which visit member countries to gather data and to provide technical assistance on debt issues. Nevertheless, quality and coverage vary among debtors and may also vary for the same debtor from year to year. Data on long-term external debt reported by member countries are checked against, and supplemented by, data from several other sources. Among these sources are the statements and reports of several regional development banks, government lending agencies, and official government websites. 244

Glossary This list provides general descriptions, not precise legal definitions, of the terms commonly used in this report. However, the descriptions include legal and policy elements relevant to how these terms are understood and applied in practice. Base year is the period against which quantities and prices of a given period are compared. Bilateral currency swap line is an agreement between two central banks to exchange a cash flow in one currency against a cash flow in another currency according to predetermined terms and conditions. Blue bond is a debt instrument issued by governments, development banks, or other entities to raise capital from impact investors to finance marine and ocean-based projects that yield positive environmental, economic, and climate benefits. Bonds are debt instruments issued by public and publicly guaranteed or private debtors with durations of one year or longer. Bonds usually give the holder the unconditional right to fixed money income or to contractually determined, variable money income.

Central bank is a country’s financial institution that exercises control over key aspects of the financial system. It carries out activities such as issuing currency, managing international reserves, transacting with the International Monetary Fund, and providing credit to deposit-taking corporations. Commitments (of public and publicly guaranteed debt) constitute the total amount of new long-term loans to public sector borrowers or to borrowers with a public sector guarantee extended by official and private lenders and for which contracts were signed in the year specified. Common Framework for debt treatment beyond the Debt Service Suspension Initiative is an initiative launched in 2022 and endorsed by the Group of Twenty, designed to support, in a structural manner, low-income countries with unsustainable debt. Concessional debt conveys information about the borrower’s receipt of aid from official lenders at concessional terms as defined by the World Bank, that is, loans with an original grant element of 35 percent or more. The World Bank classifies 247

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 loans from major regional development banks—the African Development Bank, Asian Development Bank, and Inter-American Development Bank—as concessional. Debt buyback is the repurchase by a debtor of its own debt, either at a discount price or at par value. In the event of a buyback of long-term debt, the face value of the debt bought back will be recorded as a decline in stock outstanding of long-term debt, and the cash amount received by creditors will be recorded as a principal repayment. Debt distress, as defined under the International Monetary Fund–World Bank Debt Sustainability Framework (DSF) for low-income countries, is caused by unsustainable debt, wherein a country is unable to fulfill its financial obligations and debt restructuring is required. Debt-distressed is when a country’s debt and debt service ratios significantly and persistently breach established thresholds, indicating an inability to meet the country’s financial obligations. It is the most severe risk category in the International Monetary Fund–World Bank Debt Sustainability Framework (DSF) for low-income countries.

Debt-for-climate swaps are agreements that convert debts into commitments related to climate activities. Debt-for-development swaps are agreements that convert debts into commitments related to a specific development goal, such as nature conservation, climate action, education, nutrition, or support for refugees. Debt-for-equity swaps are agreements that convert debts into commitments related to equity investments. Debt-for-nature swaps are agreements that convert debts into commitments related to conservation activities. Debt restructurings are revisions to debt service obligations agreed on by creditors and debtors. Such agreements change the amount and timing of future principal and interest payments. Debt restructuring is a complex process that requires the agreement of domestic and foreign creditors and involves burden sharing between different parties (for example, between residents and banks in most restructurings of domestic debt).

Debt service is the sum of principal repayments and interest paid on total long-term debt (public and publicly guaranteed debt and private nonguaranteed debt). Debt Service Suspension Initiative (DSSI) took effect on May 1, 2020, and allowed 73 eligible countries to apply for a temporary suspension of debt service 248

GLOssARy payments owed to official bilateral creditors. The suspension period, originally set to end on December 31, 2020, was extended through December 2021. Debt service-to-export ratio is the ratio of total debt service (principal repayments and interest payments) to the value of exports of goods and services and receipts of primary income from abroad. Debt service-to-GNI ratio is the ratio of total debt service (principal repayments and interest payments) to gross national income (GNI). Debt sustainability is the condition under which a country (or its government) does not, in the future, need to default or renegotiate or restructure its debt, or make implausibly large policy adjustments. Debt swap (conversion) is an exchange of debt—typically at a discount—for a nondebt claim (such as equity) or for counterpart funds that can be used to finance a particular project or policy. In essence, public sector debt is extinguished and a nondebt liability created in a debt conversion.

Debt-to-export ratio is the ratio of outstanding external debt to the value of exports of goods and services and receipts of primary income from abroad. Debt-to-GNI ratio is the ratio of outstanding external debt to gross national income (GNI). Debt transparency results in readily available data on public debt, allowing governments to make informed decisions about macroeconomic policy and debt sustainability. Disbursements are drawings during the year specified on loan commitments contracted by the borrower. Eurobond is a type of bond that governments or corporations issue outside of their home country and is denominated in a currency different from that of the issuer. Typically, Eurobonds are long-term debt instruments and are commonly denominated in US dollars. They can also be denominated in other currencies such as the euro, pound, Japanese yen, and Swiss franc.

External debt flows are debt-related transactions during the year specified. They include disbursements, principal repayments, and interest payments. External debt stocks comprise public and publicly guaranteed long-term external debt, private nonguaranteed long-term external debt, use of International Monetary Fund credit and special drawing rights allocation, and short-term external debt. 249

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 Fiscal sustainability refers to the future implications of current fiscal policies and, more precisely, to the question of whether the government can continue to pursue its set of budgetary policies without endangering its solvency. Foreign direct investment refers to direct investment equity flows in the reporting economy. It is the sum of equity capital, reinvestment earnings, and other capital. Direct investment is a category of cross-border investment associated with a resident in one economy having control or a significant degree of influence on the management of an enterprise that is resident in another economy. Ownership of 10 percent or more of the ordinary shares or voting stock is the criterion for determining the existence of a direct investment relationship. Fragile and conflict-affected situations (FCS) are countries with high levels of institutional and social fragility, identified using indicators that measure the quality of policy and institutions, and manifestations of fragility, and/or are countries affected by violent conflict, identified using a threshold number of conflict-related deaths relative to the population.

The Group of Seven (G-7) is the collection of seven industrialized countries— Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States—that meets annually to discuss issues such as global economic governance, international security, and, most recently, artificial intelligence. The Group of Twenty (G-20) is the collection of the world’s largest economies— Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Mexico, the Russian Federation, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, and the United States— along with the African Union and the European Union, established to discuss international economic and financial stability.

Grace period is the time between the date on which a loan is committed and the date on which the first principal payment is due. The information presented in the International Debt Statistics database is the average grace period on all public and publicly guaranteed debt committed during the specified period. Grants are legally binding commitments that obligate a specific value of funds available for disbursement for which there is no payment requirement. They include debt forgiveness grants and grants from bilateral and multilateral agencies (such as the International Development Association). Gross domestic product is the sum of gross value added by all resident producers in the economy, plus any product taxes and minus any subsidies not included in the value of the products. 250

GLOssARy Gross national income is the sum of value added by all resident producers, plus any product taxes (less subsidies) not included in the valuation of output, plus net receipts of primary income compensation of employees and property income from abroad. Yearly average exchange rates are used to convert gross national income from local currency to US dollars. Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) Initiative is a program of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund to provide debt relief to qualifying countries with unsustainable debt burdens. IDA-eligible countries are the countries that are eligible to receive International Development Association (IDA) resources. Eligibility for IDA support depends on a country’s relative poverty, defined as gross national income per capita below an established threshold, which is updated annually. Inflation is the rate of increase in prices over a given period in an economy. Interest payments are the amounts of interest paid in foreign currency, goods, or services in the year specified. Interest payment-to-GNI ratio is the ratio of interest payment to gross national income (GNI).

Interest rate is the interest rate applicable to a loan commitment as specified in the loan contract. The information presented in the International Debt Statistics database is the average interest on all public and publicly guaranteed debt committed during the specified period. Long-term external debt is debt that has an original or extended maturity of more than one year and that is owed to nonresidents by residents of an economy and is repayable in currency, goods, or services. Maturity is the date on which the final principal repayment on a loan is due. It is the sum of the grace and repayment periods. The information presented in the International Debt Statistics database is the average maturity on all public and publicly guaranteed debt committed during the specified period. Monetary policy is used by central banks to manage economic fluctuations and achieve price stability, with low and stable inflation. Central banks conduct monetary policy by adjusting the supply of money, usually through buying or selling securities in the open market. When central banks lower interest rates, monetary policy is easing. When they raise interest rates, monetary policy is tightening.
Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative (MDRI) is a program of the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the Inter-American Development Bank, and 251

INTERNATIONAL DEBT REPORT 2026 the African Development Bank that provides additional debt relief to countries that have completed the Heavily Indebted Poor Countries Initiative process. Multilateral official creditors are official agencies owned or governed by more than one country that provide loan financing. They include international financial institutions such as the World Bank, regional development banks, and other intergovernmental agencies. Multilateral-to-external debt stock is the ratio of the stock of debt owed to multilateral creditors to total external debt. Net debt flow is gross disbursements minus principal payments. Net transfers on external debt are net flows minus interest payments during the year; negative transfers show net transfers made by the borrower to the creditor during the year. Official creditor committee is a group formed to represent the collective interests of creditors during the debt restructuring or bankruptcy process of a debtor, typically a corporation or sovereign entity.

Official creditors are governments or other bilateral public entities (such as export-import agencies or development agencies) and multilateral financial institutions (such as the World Bank and regional development banks). Paris Club is an informal group of official creditors whose role is to find coordinated and sustainable solutions to the payment difficulties experienced by debtor countries. Paris Club creditors provide appropriate debt treatment as debtor countries undertake reforms to stabilize and restore their macroeconomic and financial situations. Principal repayments are the amounts of principal (amortization) paid in currency, goods, or services in the year specified with respect to long-term external debt. Private creditors are bondholders, commercial banks, and other trade-related lenders. Private nonguaranteed debt is debt owed by private sector borrowers to external creditors on loans that do not benefit from a public sector guarantee by the debtor country.

Public and publicly guaranteed debt comprises public debt (an external obligation of a public debtor, such as the general government or agency, the central bank, a political subdivision or agency, or an autonomous public body) and publicly guaranteed external debt (an external obligation of a private debtor that is guaranteed for repayment by a public entity). 252

GLOssARy Public debt is an external obligation of a public debtor, including all levels of government, the central bank, state-owned enterprises, public corporations, development banks, and any other autonomous public bodies of government. Public domestic debt comprises debt liabilities owed by public sector entities to other resident units of the same economy. SDR allocations are reserve-related liabilities, distributed to member countries in proportion to their quota shares at the International Monetary Fund. The SDR (special drawing right) allocations are included in the gross external debt position and classified as long-term special drawing rights. Short-term external debt has an original maturity of one year or less. Available data permit no distinctions among public, publicly guaranteed, and private nonguaranteed short-term external debt. State-owned enterprise is a corporate entity recognized by law that is at least partially owned by the government.

Total Return Swap is a financial derivative contract under which one party transfers the total economic return of a reference asset to another party in exchange for a predetermined stream of payments. The total return typically includes both periodic income generated by the asset, such as interest or coupon payments, and any capital gains or losses resulting from changes in the market value of the asset over the life of the contract. Treasury bonds are long-term debt securities with a maturity period of 20 or 30 years. They are considered low-risk and are generally free of risk when held until maturity. Variable-rate loans are loans for which the interest fluctuates according to changes in market interest rates. 253

For more than five decades, the World Bank’s premier annual publication on debt, now titled the International Debt Report (IDR), along with the associated International Debt Statistics (IDS) database, has helped shape policies in development finance by sharing timely and comprehensive external debt data and analysis with the international community. Drawing on data collected through the World Bank’s Debtor Reporting System, this publication has kept pace with evolving borrowing patterns and new lending instruments, measured the impact of initiatives to relieve debt burdens, and promoted best practices in debt recording and reporting. Each year the report presents an analysis of evolving trends in external debt stocks and flows of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), as well as issues and challenges for development finance. The IDS database provides comprehensive information on external debt stocks and flows of public and private borrowers in LMICs (by borrower and creditor), the terms on which external loans are contracted, current and future debt service, and debt indicators in relation to key economic variables. IDR 2026 encompasses

• Analysis of external debt stocks and flows for 2015–25; • Debt dynamics and the policy implications; • Advancing debt transparency; and • A one-page summary for each country, plus global, regional, and income group aggregates showing debt stocks and flows, relevant debt indicators, and average terms on new commitments.
